clinicalNotes: May-Thurner syndrome, where the right iliac artery compresses the left iliac vein against the spine, is an underdiagnosed cause of left-leg deep vein thrombosis.

descriptionProfessional: The deep vein of the thigh, running alongside the femoral artery, receiving the great saphenous vein before passing under the inguinal ligament to become the external iliac vein.
descriptionPatient: The main deep vein in your thigh that carries blood from your leg back toward your heart.
apBiologyFacts: It sits medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle - the reverse of the arm, where the vein position varies - which matters for anyone learning to find venous access.
clinicalNotes: Deep vein thrombosis here is dangerous because a clot that breaks free travels directly to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.
It's a common site for femoral venous catheter placement in critically ill patients.

descriptionProfessional: Drains the leg's deep veins behind the knee, becoming the femoral vein as it passes through the adductor hiatus.
descriptionPatient: The vein behind your knee that carries blood from your lower leg back up toward your heart.
apBiologyFacts: Most calf deep vein thromboses form in the smaller veins below this point and are watched closely because propagation up into the popliteal vein raises embolism risk substantially.
clinicalNotes: Compression ultrasound of this vein and the femoral vein is the standard test to rule out proximal deep vein thrombosis.

descriptionProfessional: The longest vein in the body, running superficially from the medial ankle up the entire length of the leg to join the femoral vein in the groin. Contains multiple one-way valves.
descriptionPatient: The longest vein in your body - it runs just under the skin along the inside of your whole leg, from your ankle to your groin.
apBiologyFacts: It is the longest vein in the human body, and being superficial (just under the skin, not deep in muscle) is exactly why it's so easy to see bulging when its valves fail.

Its one-way valves rely on the calf muscle pump (contracting leg muscles squeezing blood upward against gravity) to keep blood moving toward the heart; standing still for long periods lets blood pool here.
Because it's long, superficial, and expendable (the deep veins can handle the leg's venous return alone), it is the vessel most often harvested for coronary artery bypass grafts.
clinicalNotes: Varicose veins form when its valves fail, letting blood reflux and pool, stretching and bulging the vein visibly under the skin.
It's the standard graft vessel harvested for coronary artery bypass surgery, precisely because losing it causes minimal harm.
Superficial thrombophlebitis (a clot with inflammation) here is uncomfortable but far less dangerous than a deep vein thrombosis, since it's unlikely to embolize to the lungs.

descriptionProfessional: A broad fan-shaped muscle filling the temporal fossa, inserting on the mandible's coronoid process; along with the masseter, it is a primary muscle of mastication, powerful in closing and retracting the jaw.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the side of your head, above your ear, that helps you bite down and close your jaw.
apBiologyFacts: It's innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), the same nerve that gives facial skin its sensation - motor and sensory function traveling together in one cranial nerve.
Its posterior fibers run nearly horizontally, which is what lets it retract (pull backward) the jaw in addition to closing it - a job the more vertically-oriented masseter can't do as well.
clinicalNotes: You can feel it contract by placing fingers on your temple and clenching your teeth - a quick bedside test of trigeminal motor function.

descriptionProfessional: A thick, rectangular muscle running from the zygomatic arch to the mandible's angle - pound for pound one of the strongest muscles in the body for generating bite force.
descriptionPatient: The thick muscle at the back of your jaw that you can feel bulge when you clench your teeth.
apBiologyFacts: Along with the temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids, it's one of the four muscles of mastication, all supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
It can generate some of the highest force per cross-sectional area of any muscle in the body, which is why jaw-clenching (bruxism) can wear down tooth enamel over years.
clinicalNotes: Botox injected into an overactive masseter is used cosmetically to slim a square jawline and therapeutically to treat bruxism-related jaw pain.
Masseter hypertrophy from chronic teeth grinding is a common finding in TMJ (temporomandibular joint) disorder workups.

descriptionProfessional: The forehead's muscle belly, part of the occipitofrontalis muscle, raising the eyebrows and wrinkling the forehead horizontally. A muscle of facial expression, not mastication.
descriptionPatient: The muscle in your forehead that raises your eyebrows and creates the horizontal wrinkles when you look surprised.
apBiologyFacts: It belongs to the muscles of facial expression, a group unique among skeletal muscles in that most insert directly into skin rather than onto another bone - which is exactly what lets them move skin to make an expression instead of moving a joint.

It's innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), not the trigeminal - a different cranial nerve than the muscles of mastication, and testing forehead wrinkling versus jaw clench distinguishes which nerve is affected in a facial palsy.
clinicalNotes: One of the most common cosmetic targets for Botox, which weakens it to smooth forehead wrinkles.

In Bell's palsy (facial nerve paralysis), the forehead on the affected side cannot wrinkle - a key exam finding that distinguishes a peripheral facial nerve problem from a stroke, where forehead movement is often spared because it receives bilateral brain input.

descriptionProfessional: The sphincter-like muscle ring encircling each orbit, responsible for closing the eyelids, from a gentle blink to a forceful squeeze.
descriptionPatient: The ring of muscle around your eye that lets you blink and squeeze your eyes shut.
apBiologyFacts: As a true sphincter muscle, its fibers form closed rings around the eye - contracting shrinks the ring's diameter, exactly how any sphincter muscle in the body works, from the eye to the digestive tract.
It's innervated by the facial nerve, and testing whether someone can forcefully close their eyes against resistance is a standard part of assessing facial nerve function.
clinicalNotes: In facial nerve palsy, the eye on the affected side may not close fully (lagophthalmos), risking corneal drying and injury - patients often need lubricating drops or taping the eye shut at night.
Blepharospasm, involuntary spasm of this muscle, is treated with targeted Botox injections.

descriptionProfessional: The sphincter muscle ring surrounding the mouth, closing the lips and shaping them for speech, and the muscle every other facial expression muscle around the mouth ultimately pulls against.
descriptionPatient: The ring of muscle around your mouth that lets you close your lips, purse them, and shape sounds when you speak.
apBiologyFacts: Like the orbicularis oculi, it's a true sphincter - and because nearly every other muscle of the lower face (zygomaticus, buccinator, depressor anguli oris) inserts into it, it functions as the anchor point the whole lower face pulls against to form an expression.
It's essential for forming many consonant sounds in speech (like 'p', 'b', 'm') by briefly sealing the lips completely.
clinicalNotes: Weakness here from facial nerve injury causes drooling and difficulty with lip seal, both for speech clarity and for keeping food/liquid in the mouth while eating.

descriptionProfessional: Runs from the zygomatic bone to the corner of the mouth; its contraction is the principal action of smiling, pulling the mouth corner up and laterally.
descriptionPatient: The 'smile muscle' - it runs from your cheekbone to the corner of your mouth and pulls your mouth up when you smile.
apBiologyFacts: A genuine (Duchenne) smile activates both this muscle and the orbicularis oculi around the eyes together, while a purely voluntary/social smile often uses only the zygomaticus - a distinction researchers use to study whether a smile reflects real emotion.
clinicalNotes: Asymmetric smile - one side of the mouth failing to rise - is a classic sign used to screen for stroke or facial nerve palsy (the FAST stroke assessment includes exactly this: asking a patient to smile).

descriptionProfessional: A thin, deep muscle forming the wall of the cheek, compressing it against the teeth to keep food positioned between the molars while chewing, and assisting in actions like blowing.
descriptionPatient: The muscle inside your cheek that pushes food back onto your teeth while you chew, and lets you blow air out (like playing a trumpet).
apBiologyFacts: Its name comes from the Latin for 'trumpeter' - it's the muscle that lets you forcefully blow air out through pursed lips, the key muscle used by trumpet and other brass/wind instrument players.
Functionally it works as a wall, not a mover: instead of producing visible facial movement, it keeps chewed food from pooling in the cheek pouch, pushing it back between the teeth.
clinicalNotes: Weakness here after facial nerve injury causes food to collect in the cheek during eating, a common complaint after facial nerve damage or stroke.

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-T1), spiraling around the back of the humerus before supplying the extensor muscles of the forearm and sensation to the back of the hand.
descriptionPatient: A nerve running down the back of your arm that controls the muscles that straighten your wrist and fingers.
apBiologyFacts: It winds around the humerus in the spiral (radial) groove, running directly against bone - which is exactly why a mid-shaft humerus fracture is one of the classic causes of radial nerve injury.
It controls wrist and finger extension; losing it causes 'wrist drop', since the (now unopposed) flexor muscles pull the wrist into flexion with nothing to extend it back.
clinicalNotes: 'Saturday night palsy' - radial nerve compression from a heavy arm draped over a chair edge or a partner's shoulder during sleep - causes temporary wrist drop.
It's tested clinically by checking wrist and finger extension against resistance, and sensation on the back of the hand between the thumb and index finger.

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus (C6-T1), running down the arm's midline, through the carpal tunnel at the wrist, supplying most forearm flexors and thumb/finger sensation.
descriptionPatient: A nerve running down the middle of your arm and through your wrist that controls many hand movements and gives feeling to your thumb and first two fingers.
apBiologyFacts: It passes through the carpal tunnel, a narrow passage at the wrist bounded by carpal bones and a tough ligament - any swelling in that confined space compresses the nerve directly.
It supplies sensation to the thumb, index, middle, and half the ring finger - the classic distribution tested in a carpal tunnel exam.
clinicalNotes: Carpal tunnel syndrome, compression of this nerve at the wrist, is one of the most common nerve entrapment conditions, causing numbness/tingling in its sensory distribution and, if severe, thumb muscle wasting.
It runs directly under the palmaris longus tendon at the wrist, a useful surface landmark in the physical exam and in carpal tunnel release surgery.

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8-T1), running superficially behind the medial epicondyle of the elbow before supplying most intrinsic hand muscles and sensation to the little finger.
descriptionPatient: The nerve that runs behind the bony bump on the inside of your elbow - the one that gives you a shock down your arm when you hit your 'funny bone'.
apBiologyFacts: At the elbow it runs superficially, right behind the medial epicondyle with almost nothing protecting it - which is exactly the 'funny bone' spot, and exactly why a direct hit there causes that jolt of tingling down to the little finger.
It supplies most of the small intrinsic muscles of the hand, which is why long-term ulnar nerve damage causes a characteristic 'claw hand' as those small muscles weaken.
clinicalNotes: Repeated pressure on the elbow (leaning on a desk, prolonged bed rest) can cause cubital tunnel syndrome, an ulnar nerve compression injury.
It's tested by checking sensation on the little finger and the strength of finger abduction (spreading the fingers apart).

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the lumbar plexus (L2-L4), passing under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral vessels to supply the anterior thigh muscles (including the quadriceps) and sensation to the front of the thigh.
descriptionPatient: A nerve that runs down the front of your thigh and controls the muscles that let you straighten your knee.
apBiologyFacts: It innervates the quadriceps, which is why femoral nerve injury or a spinal block affecting it abolishes the knee-jerk (patellar) reflex - one of the most commonly tested deep tendon reflexes.
clinicalNotes: A femoral nerve block is commonly used for pain control after knee surgery, since it numbs the quadriceps and the front of the thigh.
It can be compressed or stretched during pelvic surgery or prolonged lithotomy positioning, causing quadriceps weakness afterward.

descriptionProfessional: The larger terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, continuing down the back of the leg through the posterior compartment to supply the calf muscles and the sole of the foot.
descriptionPatient: A nerve that runs down the back of your calf and controls the muscles that point your toes down and give feeling to the sole of your foot.
apBiologyFacts: It's one of the sciatic nerve's two terminal branches (with the common fibular nerve), splitting at or above the knee - so 'sciatica' pain can, depending on where the irritation is, affect either branch's specific territory.
clinicalNotes: Tibial nerve injury causes weakness in plantar flexion (pointing the toes down) and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot, which is a serious problem for diabetic patients since they may not feel a foot injury forming.

descriptionProfessional: The smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, winding superficially around the neck of the fibula before splitting into deep and superficial branches supplying the muscles that lift the foot.
descriptionPatient: A nerve that wraps around the outside of your knee, just below the surface - the one responsible for 'foot drop' if it gets injured.
apBiologyFacts: It winds directly around the neck of the fibula with almost nothing but skin protecting it, exactly like the ulnar nerve at the elbow - both are textbook examples of a nerve made vulnerable purely by running superficially over bone.
clinicalNotes: It's the nerve most often injured by a tight leg cast, prolonged kneeling, or crossing the legs for a long time, causing 'foot drop' - inability to lift the front of the foot, producing a high-stepping gait.
Foot drop from this nerve's injury is a classic finding tested in any lower-limb neurological exam.

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the sacral plexus (S2-S4), supplying motor control to the pelvic floor and external anal/urethral sphincters, and sensation to the perineum.
descriptionPatient: A nerve in your pelvis that controls the muscles you use to hold in urine and stool, and carries feeling from that area.
apBiologyFacts: It carries the somatic (voluntary) motor supply to the external anal and urethral sphincters - which is why voluntarily holding urine or stool, unlike most digestive/urinary function, is under conscious control.
clinicalNotes: A pudendal nerve block is used during childbirth and some pelvic procedures to numb the perineum.
Chronic compression (e.g. from prolonged cycling) can cause pudendal neuralgia, a painful condition affecting the perineum.

descriptionProfessional: The second cranial nerve, carrying visual signals from the retina to the brain's visual processing centers; technically a tract of the central nervous system rather than a true peripheral nerve.
descriptionPatient: The nerve that carries what your eye sees to your brain, letting you see.
apBiologyFacts: Unlike every other cranial nerve, it is actually an extension of the brain itself (central nervous system tissue, wrapped in the same meninges as the brain), not a true peripheral nerve - which is why it can't regenerate if damaged, unlike most peripheral nerves.

The two optic nerves partially cross at the optic chiasm, so each half of the brain ends up processing the opposite half of the combined visual field from both eyes - the anatomical basis for stereoscopic depth perception.
clinicalNotes: A doctor examines it directly with an ophthalmoscope, looking at the optic disc - the only place in the body where a nerve and blood vessels can be viewed directly without surgery.
Optic nerve swelling (papilledema) is a sign of raised intracranial pressure, visible on this direct exam before other symptoms may appear.
Multiple sclerosis often first presents as optic neuritis - sudden vision loss from demyelination of this nerve.

descriptionProfessional: The fifth and largest cranial nerve, with three divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) carrying facial sensation and providing motor supply to the muscles of mastication.
descriptionPatient: The main nerve that gives feeling to your face, and also controls the muscles you use to chew.
apBiologyFacts: It has both sensory and motor roles in one nerve: sensory for nearly all facial skin sensation via its three divisions, and motor specifically for the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, pterygoids) - a combination most cranial nerves don't have.
Its three divisions - ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), mandibular (V3) - map to horizontal bands of the face, a pattern used clinically to localize facial sensory loss.
clinicalNotes: Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe, electric-shock-like facial pain along one of its divisions, often triggered by something as light as touching the face or brushing teeth.
The corneal reflex (blinking when the cornea is touched) tests this nerve's sensory limb (V1) paired with the facial nerve's motor limb.

descriptionProfessional: The seventh cranial nerve, providing motor supply to all the muscles of facial expression, taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and parasympathetic supply to several glands.
descriptionPatient: The nerve that controls all the muscles you use to make facial expressions, like smiling, frowning, and closing your eyes.
apBiologyFacts: It supplies every muscle of facial expression on its side of the face - a single nerve controlling an entire face's worth of movement, which is why its injury (Bell's palsy) is so visually obvious.

The upper face (forehead) receives motor input from both sides of the brain, but the lower face only from the opposite side - the anatomical reason a stroke typically spares the forehead while paralyzing the lower face, while a peripheral facial nerve injury (Bell's palsy) paralyzes the whole side, forehead included.
clinicalNotes: Bell's palsy, an acute peripheral facial nerve palsy (often linked to viral reactivation), paralyzes an entire side of the face - forehead included - distinguishing it from a stroke, which typically spares forehead movement.
Testing whether a patient can raise their eyebrows is the single fastest bedside way to tell a peripheral facial nerve problem from a central (stroke) one.

descriptionProfessional: Arises from the cervical plexus (C3-C5), descending through the neck and thorax to provide the diaphragm's sole motor supply.
descriptionPatient: The nerve that controls your diaphragm, the main muscle you use to breathe - so it's essential for every breath you take.
apBiologyFacts: It is the diaphragm's only motor supply, and the diaphragm does the majority of the work of quiet breathing - which is why 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive' is a standard memory aid for its spinal cord origin.

It travels an unusually long path from the neck all the way down to the diaphragm - a leftover of embryonic development, when the diaphragm's muscle originates high in the neck region and migrates downward during development, dragging its nerve supply along with it.
clinicalNotes: A high spinal cord injury above C3-C5 can paralyze the diaphragm entirely, requiring mechanical ventilation.

Referred shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation (e.g. from blood or gas under the diaphragm after surgery) happens because the phrenic nerve's spinal cord level (C3-C5) overlaps with the shoulder's sensory nerve supply.

descriptionProfessional: The anterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves (T1-T11), running along the lower border of each rib to supply the intercostal muscles and skin of the chest and upper abdominal wall.
descriptionPatient: The nerves that run along your ribs, controlling the muscles between them that help you breathe and giving feeling to your chest wall.
apBiologyFacts: Each one runs in a neurovascular bundle with an intercostal artery and vein, tucked just under the lower edge of its rib - a fixed, testable anatomical order (vein, artery, nerve, top to bottom) that determines exactly where a needle is safely inserted between ribs.
Because they map cleanly to specific spinal cord levels, the pattern of chest wall sensation they carry is used clinically to determine the level of a spinal cord injury.
clinicalNotes: A needle placed between ribs (for a chest tube or thoracentesis) is inserted along the top of the lower rib specifically to avoid the nerve and vessels tucked under the rib above.
Shingles (herpes zoster) reactivating in an intercostal nerve's sensory ganglion causes a band of painful blistering rash following that one nerve's exact territory around the chest wall.

descriptionProfessional: The single bone forming the forehead and the roof of both orbits. It contains the frontal sinuses and articulates with the parietal bones at the coronal suture.
descriptionPatient: The bone of your forehead, which also forms the top of your eye sockets.
apBiologyFacts: Flat bones of the skull form by intramembranous ossification - bone laid down directly in membrane, with no cartilage model first - unlike long bones, which ossify from cartilage (endochondral).

In a newborn the frontal bone is two halves separated by the metopic suture, and the anterior fontanelle (soft spot) sits where it meets the parietals; the fontanelle closes at about 18-24 months, letting the skull deform during birth and the brain grow after it.
The frontal sinuses are air-filled cavities that lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.
clinicalNotes: The pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet, is the thinnest part of the side of the skull and overlies the middle meningeal artery; a blow here can cause an epidural hematoma.
A fracture through the frontal sinus can tear the dura and leak cerebrospinal fluid from the nose.
Frontal sinusitis causes pain and pressure above the eyes, worse on leaning forward.

descriptionProfessional: Paired quadrilateral bones forming most of the roof and upper sides of the cranial vault, joined at the midline by the sagittal suture.
descriptionPatient: Two large curved bones that make up the top and sides of your skull.
apBiologyFacts: The parietal bones meet each other at the sagittal suture, the frontal bone at the coronal suture, the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture and the temporal bone at the squamous suture - sutures are immovable fibrous joints (synarthroses).
Bone in the skull vault is a sandwich: two layers of compact bone around spongy bone (diploe), a light, strong design that also absorbs impact.
The inner surface carries a groove for the middle meningeal artery, which is why this bone matters clinically.
clinicalNotes: Fracture of the parietal or temporal bone can rupture the middle meningeal artery, causing an epidural hematoma: a brief lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration, seen on CT as a biconvex (lens-shaped) bleed.
Premature fusion of the sagittal suture (craniosynostosis) produces a long, narrow head (scaphocephaly).
Cephalohematoma, a collection of blood under the periosteum of a parietal bone, is common after a difficult delivery and never crosses a suture line.

descriptionProfessional: The single bone forming the back and part of the base of the skull. Its foramen magnum transmits the brainstem-spinal cord junction, and its two condyles articulate with the atlas.
descriptionPatient: The bone at the back and base of your skull, with the big hole where your spinal cord passes up into your brain.
apBiologyFacts: The foramen magnum ('great hole') passes the medulla oblongata becoming the spinal cord, the vertebral arteries and the spinal accessory nerve roots.
The occipital condyles fit into the atlas (C1) to form the atlanto-occipital joint, a hinge that lets you nod 'yes'.
The external occipital protuberance (inion) is the bump at the back of the head; strong neck muscles and the nuchal ligament anchor here.
clinicalNotes: If raised pressure pushes the cerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum (tonsillar herniation), the medulla is compressed and breathing and heart rate fail - the reason lumbar puncture is avoided when pressure is suspected to be high.
A basilar skull fracture, through the base of the occipital and temporal bones, can show as bruising behind the ear (Battle sign) or around the eyes (raccoon eyes).
Chiari malformation is a congenital descent of cerebellar tissue through the foramen magnum.

descriptionProfessional: Paired bones forming the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each houses the middle and inner ear, bears the mastoid and styloid processes, and forms the socket for the jaw joint.
descriptionPatient: The bone at the side of your head around your ear. It holds the delicate parts of your ear inside it.
apBiologyFacts: Each temporal bone contains the organs of hearing and balance: the three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes - the smallest bones in the body), the cochlea and the semicircular canals.
Sound is transduced in the cochlea, where vibration bends hair cells whose stereocilia open ion channels, turning mechanical energy into nerve impulses along the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).
The mastoid process is filled with air cells connected to the middle ear, and is the attachment for the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
clinicalNotes: Mastoiditis is infection spreading from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells.
The facial nerve (CN VII) runs through the temporal bone, so a fracture here can cause facial paralysis and hearing loss, with fluid leaking from the ear.
Conductive hearing loss involves the outer or middle ear; sensorineural loss involves the cochlea or its nerve - a tuning fork against the mastoid (Rinne test) separates them.

descriptionProfessional: The butterfly-shaped keystone of the skull base, articulating with every other cranial bone. It bears the sella turcica, which houses the pituitary gland, and contains the sphenoid sinus.
descriptionPatient: A butterfly-shaped bone deep in the middle of your skull that holds all the other skull bones together.
apBiologyFacts: It is the only cranial bone that touches all the others, which is why it is called the keystone of the cranium.
The sella turcica ('Turkish saddle') cradles the pituitary gland, the 'master gland' whose hormones regulate the thyroid, adrenals, gonads and growth.
Openings in the sphenoid pass the optic nerve (optic canal) and the nerves that move the eye (superior orbital fissure: CN III, IV, V1, VI).
clinicalNotes: A pituitary tumour can enlarge the sella and press on the optic chiasm above it, classically causing bitemporal hemianopia - loss of the outer half of each visual field.
Surgeons often remove pituitary tumours through the nose and the sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal approach), avoiding opening the skull.
The greater wing forms part of the pterion, the weak point over the middle meningeal artery.

descriptionProfessional: The paired cheekbone, forming the prominence of the cheek and the lateral wall and floor of the orbit. It joins the temporal bone to make the zygomatic arch.
descriptionPatient: Your cheekbone, which gives your face its shape and forms the outer edge of the eye socket.
apBiologyFacts: The zygomatic arch, formed by the zygomatic and temporal bones, is the attachment for the masseter, one of the strongest chewing muscles.
Facial bones, like the skull vault, are formed by intramembranous ossification, and the face grows most during childhood as the sinuses and teeth develop.
Its thin lateral projection is a common palpation landmark: you can feel the arch running back to just in front of the ear.
clinicalNotes: A blow to the cheek can produce a tripod (zygomaticomaxillary complex) fracture, flattening the cheek and often damaging the infraorbital nerve, so the cheek and upper lip go numb.
Fractures involving the orbital floor can trap the muscle that lifts the eye, causing double vision on looking up.

descriptionProfessional: The paired upper jaw bones, fused at the midline. They bear the upper teeth, form the hard palate, the floor of the orbit and the sides of the nasal aperture, and contain the maxillary sinuses.
descriptionPatient: Your upper jaw. It holds your upper teeth and forms the roof of your mouth.
apBiologyFacts: The palatine processes of the two maxillae join at the midline to form the hard palate, separating the mouth from the nasal cavity so you can breathe and chew at once.
The maxillary sinus is the largest of the paranasal sinuses; these air spaces warm and humidify air, lighten the skull and add resonance to speech.
Teeth sit in sockets (alveoli) in the alveolar process, held by fibrous joints called gomphoses.
clinicalNotes: Cleft palate results from the palatine processes failing to fuse during weeks 6-12 of development; it interferes with feeding and speech.
The roots of upper molars project close to the maxillary sinus floor, so a dental infection can cause sinusitis, and extraction can open a channel between mouth and sinus.
Le Fort fractures classify midface fractures by the level at which the maxilla separates from the skull.

descriptionProfessional: Two small rectangular bones that meet at the midline to form the bridge of the nose. The rest of the external nose is cartilage.
descriptionPatient: The two small bones that form the hard bridge of your nose.
apBiologyFacts: Only the upper nose is bone; the flexible lower part is hyaline cartilage, which is why the tip of the nose bends and the bridge does not.
The nasal cavity is divided by a septum of bone (vomer, ethmoid) and cartilage; its lining warms, humidifies and filters inspired air.
Olfactory receptors, the neurons for smell, lie in the roof of the nasal cavity.
clinicalNotes: They are the most commonly fractured facial bones.
After nasal trauma a septal hematoma - blood collected under the septal lining - must be drained promptly, or the cartilage loses its blood supply and collapses (saddle nose).
A deviated septum can obstruct airflow on one side.

descriptionProfessional: Thirty-two permanent teeth (20 deciduous in childhood): 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars. Each has an enamel crown over dentin, a pulp cavity with nerves and vessels, and a root held in its socket by the periodontal ligament.
descriptionPatient: Your 32 adult teeth, which cut and grind food so you can digest it.
apBiologyFacts: Digestion begins mechanically in the mouth: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind, increasing food's surface area for enzymes.
Enamel is the hardest substance in the body (about 96% hydroxyapatite mineral) but is acellular - once lost, it cannot regenerate.
Humans are diphyodont: 20 deciduous teeth are replaced by 32 permanent ones. The third molars (wisdom teeth) erupt last, in the late teens or twenties.
clinicalNotes: Dental caries is decay caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans fermenting sugar to acid, which dissolves enamel.
Periodontitis, inflammation destroying the ligament and bone around teeth, is the leading cause of adult tooth loss and is linked to cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
Impacted third molars are removed if they cause pain, infection or crowding.

descriptionProfessional: A small U-shaped bone in the anterior neck, below the mandible and above the larynx. It is the only bone in the body that articulates with no other bone, suspended by muscles and ligaments.
descriptionPatient: A little horseshoe-shaped bone in your neck that anchors your tongue and helps you swallow.
apBiologyFacts: It anchors the tongue above and the larynx below, and rises when you swallow, helping to close the airway over the larynx.
Uniquely, it does not join any other bone - it floats, held only by muscle and ligament, which lets the tongue and larynx move freely for speech and swallowing.
It develops from the second and third pharyngeal (branchial) arches, an embryological link to the gills of fish ancestors.
clinicalNotes: A fractured hyoid is a classic finding in strangulation, and pathologists look for it specifically.
The thyroglossal duct cyst, a midline neck swelling left from the thyroid's embryological descent, moves upward when the tongue is stuck out because of its attachment to the hyoid.

descriptionProfessional: The first cervical vertebra: a ring with no body or spinous process, carrying the skull on its two lateral masses.
descriptionPatient: The top bone of your spine. It holds up your skull, like the Greek titan Atlas holding up the sky.
apBiologyFacts: It has no vertebral body: during development the body of C1 fuses onto C2 and becomes the dens (odontoid process) of the axis.
Its upper surfaces cup the occipital condyles, forming the atlanto-occipital joint - the hinge for nodding 'yes'.
The vertebral arteries loop over its posterior arch on their way to the brain.
clinicalNotes: A Jefferson fracture, a burst of the atlas ring, follows an axial blow to the head such as a diving accident.
Because the spinal canal is wide at this level, an atlas fracture may not damage the cord, whereas a fracture of the dens beneath it is more dangerous.

descriptionProfessional: The second cervical vertebra, bearing the dens (odontoid process), a bony peg rising from its body around which the atlas rotates.
descriptionPatient: The second bone of your spine, with a peg that lets your head turn from side to side.
apBiologyFacts: The atlas pivots on the dens, so this atlantoaxial joint allows the rotation that lets you shake your head 'no'; about half of neck rotation happens here.
The dens is held against the front of the atlas by the transverse ligament, keeping it away from the spinal cord.
It is the first vertebra with a spinous process, which is large and bifid.
clinicalNotes: A hangman's fracture (bilateral fracture of the pars interarticularis of C2) results from hyperextension, as in a hanging or a head-on car collision.
Odontoid fractures are among the commonest cervical injuries in older adults after falls.
In rheumatoid arthritis, erosion of the transverse ligament can make the atlantoaxial joint unstable, threatening the cord.

descriptionProfessional: The five typical cervical vertebrae: small bodies, bifid spinous processes (except C7), and a foramen in each transverse process that transmits the vertebral artery.
descriptionPatient: The five small bones of your neck, below the top two, that let you bend and turn your head.
apBiologyFacts: The cervical spine has seven vertebrae in almost all mammals, including giraffes and mice - a striking conservation of body plan.
The transverse foramina protect the vertebral arteries, which run up through them to supply the brain stem and cerebellum.
The neck curves forward (cervical lordosis), a secondary curve that develops when an infant learns to lift its head.
clinicalNotes: Whiplash injury stretches the neck's ligaments and muscles in a sudden flexion-extension.
Spinal injury at or above C3-C5 is life-threatening because the phrenic nerve, which drives the diaphragm, arises from C3-C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive').
C7, the vertebra prominens, has the long spinous process you feel at the base of your neck.

descriptionProfessional: The twelve vertebrae of the chest, each with facets for a rib, long downward-sloping spinous processes, and a limited range of movement because of the rib cage.
descriptionPatient: The twelve bones of your upper and middle back, each one joined to a pair of ribs.
apBiologyFacts: Each thoracic vertebra articulates with a pair of ribs at costal facets, so the ribcage and spine form one structure that protects the heart and lungs.
The thoracic spine curves backward (kyphosis), a primary curve present from birth - the spine's four curves increase its strength and shock absorption.
The long, overlapping spinous processes limit extension of the chest region.
clinicalNotes: Osteoporotic compression fractures most often occur at the thoracolumbar junction (T12-L1), causing height loss and a stooped 'dowager's hump'.
Scoliosis is a sideways curvature with rotation, commonly appearing in adolescent girls.
Excessive kyphosis can result from osteoporosis or Scheuermann's disease.

descriptionProfessional: The five large vertebrae of the lower back, with massive bodies that bear the weight of the trunk and short, thick spinous processes.
descriptionPatient: The five large bones of your lower back that carry most of your body's weight.
apBiologyFacts: Their bodies are the largest in the spine because they carry the most weight, an example of structure matching function - bone mass increases where stress is greatest.
The lower back curves inward (lumbar lordosis), a secondary curve that develops when a child begins to walk upright and puts the trunk's weight over the pelvis.
The spinal cord ends at about L1-L2 (the conus medullaris), and below it the nerve roots hang as the cauda equina.
clinicalNotes: A lumbar puncture is done between L3-L4 or L4-L5, below the end of the cord, so the needle can sample cerebrospinal fluid without hitting it.
Disc herniation is commonest at L4-L5 and L5-S1 and can compress the nerve roots that form the sciatic nerve, causing sciatica.
Low back pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide; spondylolisthesis is forward slippage of one vertebra on another.

descriptionProfessional: Five fused vertebrae forming a wedge between the two hip bones, the posterior wall of the pelvis. Paired foramina on the front and back transmit the sacral nerves.
descriptionPatient: A triangular bone at the base of your spine, made of five vertebrae fused together, that locks into your pelvis.
apBiologyFacts: Five separate sacral vertebrae fuse between about age 16 and the mid-twenties; the sacrum is the keystone that transmits the weight of the trunk to the pelvis and legs.
The sacral promontory, the forward edge of S1, is a landmark used in measuring the birth canal.
In females the sacrum is generally wider and less curved, part of the wider pelvic outlet adapted for childbirth.
clinicalNotes: Pressure ulcers form over the sacrum in bedridden patients because skin is thin over bone here.
Epidural anaesthesia can be given through the sacral hiatus (a caudal block).
The sacroiliac joints between the sacrum and ilia can be a source of low back pain.

descriptionProfessional: Three to five small fused vertebrae at the bottom of the spine: the vestigial remnant of a tail.
descriptionPatient: Your tailbone, the small bone at the very bottom of your spine.
apBiologyFacts: It is a vestigial structure - a remnant of the tail of ancestors - and is evidence of common descent, along with the appendix and the muscles that wiggle the ears.
Although vestigial as a tail, it still anchors muscles and ligaments of the pelvic floor, including part of gluteus maximus and the anal sphincter.
Human embryos have a true tail at about week 5, which regresses as the coccygeal vertebrae fuse.
clinicalNotes: Coccydynia (tailbone pain) usually follows a fall onto the buttocks or childbirth, and is worse when sitting.
A coccyx can be fractured or dislocated during delivery.

descriptionProfessional: Fibrocartilage pads between adjacent vertebrae: a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gelatinous inner nucleus pulposus. There are 23 in the spine, making up about a quarter of its length.
descriptionPatient: Cushions between the bones of your spine that absorb shock and let your back bend.
apBiologyFacts: The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the embryonic notochord, and acts as a fluid-filled ball bearing while the annulus fibrosus resists tension.

Discs are avascular: nutrients diffuse in from the adjacent vertebrae, so they heal poorly, and they lose water with age, which is why people are slightly shorter in the evening and shrink as they age.
The discs, plus the four spinal curves, act as shock absorbers so that walking and jumping do not jolt the skull and brain.
clinicalNotes: A herniated disc occurs when the nucleus pulposus bulges through a tear in the annulus, most often at L4-L5 or L5-S1, and compresses a nerve root, causing radiating pain (sciatica) and numbness.
Degenerative disc disease is a normal part of ageing that becomes symptomatic in some people.
MRI is the best test for a suspected herniation; most resolve without surgery.

descriptionProfessional: The upper seven pairs of ribs, each attached at the back to a thoracic vertebra and at the front directly to the sternum by its own costal cartilage.
descriptionPatient: The top seven pairs of ribs, which connect all the way round from your spine to your breastbone.
apBiologyFacts: Breathing depends on the ribs: the intercostal muscles and diaphragm raise the ribs in a 'pump-handle' and 'bucket-handle' motion, enlarging the chest so pressure falls and air flows in.
The ribcage protects the heart, lungs and great vessels while remaining flexible enough to expand with each breath.
Ribs contain red bone marrow, which makes blood cells in adults.
clinicalNotes: Rib fractures are common after chest trauma, most often ribs 4-9, and are very painful because every breath moves them.
Multiple fractures in the same ribs can produce a flail segment that moves paradoxically with breathing.
The first rib is short and broad; the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus cross over it, so it is involved in thoracic outlet syndrome.

descriptionProfessional: Ribs 8 to 10, which join the costal cartilage of the rib above rather than the sternum, forming the costal margin.
descriptionPatient: The next three pairs of ribs, which join to the cartilage of the rib above instead of directly to the breastbone.
apBiologyFacts: Their cartilages fuse into the costal margin, the lower edge of the ribcage, which allows the lower chest to expand flexibly.
Because they attach indirectly, the lower ribs are more mobile than the upper ones.
clinicalNotes: A fracture of the lower right ribs can lacerate the liver, and of the left the spleen - so lower rib injuries are checked for internal bleeding.
The costal margin is where a doctor feels for an enlarged liver or spleen.

descriptionProfessional: The lowest two rib pairs, attached only to the vertebrae behind and ending free in the muscle of the flank.
descriptionPatient: The bottom two pairs of ribs, which are attached to your spine but not at the front.
apBiologyFacts: They are short and end freely, with no cartilage connection to the sternum or to another rib.
They protect the upper part of the kidneys at the back, a deep organ with little other bony cover.
clinicalNotes: A fracture of the 11th or 12th rib raises the suspicion of injury to the kidney.
The 12th rib is a landmark for the flank incision used in kidney surgery.

descriptionProfessional: Bars of hyaline cartilage joining the front ends of the ribs to the sternum or to the cartilage above.
descriptionPatient: Flexible cartilage that connects the front of your ribs to your breastbone.
apBiologyFacts: Hyaline cartilage is avascular, made of chondrocytes in lacunae within a collagen matrix that is smooth and resilient - the same tissue that covers joint surfaces.
Its elasticity lets the chest expand and recoil with breathing; it stiffens and calcifies with age, making the chest less compliant.
Cartilage heals slowly because it has no blood supply.
clinicalNotes: Costochondritis, inflammation of costal cartilage, causes chest wall pain that is reproduced by pressing on the joints, and can mimic a heart attack.
CPR compressions can fracture ribs and cartilage; that is an acceptable price for restoring circulation.

descriptionProfessional: The lateral, thumb-side bone of the forearm. Its small head pivots at the elbow, and its broad distal end forms most of the wrist joint with the carpal bones.
descriptionPatient: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It turns your palm up or down.
apBiologyFacts: Pronation and supination happen when the radius rotates around the ulna: the radial head spins against the capitulum while the distal end sweeps across the fixed ulna.
In the anatomical position the radius is lateral; in pronation it crosses over the ulna, making an X.
The radius bears most of the load from the hand, which is why it is broader distally and more often broken.
clinicalNotes: A Colles fracture - a break of the distal radius with dorsal displacement, the 'dinner fork' deformity - is the typical injury after falling on an outstretched hand.
The radial pulse is felt at the wrist where the radial artery passes over the distal radius.
'Nursemaid's elbow', subluxation of the radial head, occurs in toddlers pulled by the hand.

descriptionProfessional: The medial, little-finger-side bone of the forearm. Its olecranon forms the point of the elbow, and its trochlear notch grips the humerus to form the hinge of the elbow.
descriptionPatient: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. Its top end is the point of your elbow.
apBiologyFacts: The elbow is a hinge: the ulna's trochlear notch fits over the humeral trochlea, allowing flexion and extension in one plane only.
The olecranon is the lever arm of the triceps, which inserts here to extend the elbow.
The ulna is the stable bone of the forearm; the radius rotates around it.
clinicalNotes: A fall on the point of the elbow may fracture the olecranon, which the triceps then pulls apart.
The 'funny bone' is not the ulna but the ulnar nerve passing behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, right next to it.
A Monteggia fracture combines an ulnar shaft fracture with dislocation of the radial head.

descriptionProfessional: Eight small bones arranged in two rows of four: the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform proximally; the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate distally.
descriptionPatient: The eight small bones of your wrist, which let your hand bend and tilt in many directions.
apBiologyFacts: A common mnemonic for the carpals, from thumb side, is 'So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb': scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium.
Many small bones instead of one big one give the wrist its wide range of movement, and spread forces across many joints.
The carpals and the flexor retinaculum form the carpal tunnel through which the median nerve and nine tendons pass.
clinicalNotes: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal. Tenderness in the 'anatomical snuffbox' after a fall suggests it, and it may not show on the first X-ray.
Its blood supply enters from the distal end, so a fracture through the waist can cause avascular necrosis of the proximal part.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve in the tunnel, causing numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers.

descriptionProfessional: Five long bones forming the skeleton of the palm, numbered I-V from the thumb. Their heads form the knuckles.
descriptionPatient: The five bones in the palm of your hand. The knuckles are their rounded ends.
apBiologyFacts: The thumb's metacarpal is set at an angle to the rest, which along with its saddle joint at the wrist gives the thumb opposition - touching the tip to each finger.
Opposable thumbs, combined with a precision grip, are a defining adaptation of primates and let humans manipulate tools.
Each is a long bone with a base, shaft and head, ossifying with growth plates at one end only.
clinicalNotes: A boxer's fracture is a break of the neck of the fifth metacarpal from punching something hard.
The first metacarpal base fracture (Bennett fracture) is an unstable injury of the thumb.
Rheumatoid arthritis commonly attacks the knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joints.

descriptionProfessional: Fourteen bones in each hand: three in each finger (proximal, middle, distal) and two in the thumb.
descriptionPatient: The bones of your fingers - three in each finger and two in the thumb.
apBiologyFacts: The thumb has two phalanges, and each finger three: 14 in each hand, 28 in both.
Humans have an opposable thumb; the fingers' long levers and many joints give precise control, operated by tendons whose muscles lie in the forearm.
Fingertips carry the highest density of touch receptors in the body (Meissner's corpuscles), which is why two-point discrimination is finest there.
clinicalNotes: Mallet finger is a rupture of the extensor tendon at the tip of a finger, from a ball hitting it, leaving the tip drooped.
Dupuytren's contracture thickens the palmar fascia and pulls the ring and little fingers into a curl.
Clubbing is enlargement of the fingertips seen in chronic lung and heart disease.

descriptionProfessional: The bone that transmits body weight from the tibia to the foot. It has no muscular attachments and sits between the tibia and fibula above and the calcaneus below.
descriptionPatient: The ankle bone that sits between your shin and your heel and carries your weight.
apBiologyFacts: The talus sits in the ankle mortise formed by the tibia and fibula and allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, so it is essential for walking.
It has no muscle or tendon attachments and is largely covered with articular cartilage, so its blood supply is precarious.
Body weight passes tibia to talus, then divides between heel (calcaneus) and forefoot.
clinicalNotes: A fracture of the talar neck risks avascular necrosis of the body of the talus because blood enters through the neck.
A high-energy fall, or a motor accident with the foot on the brake, can fracture it.
Most ankle sprains injure the ligaments around the talus, especially the anterior talofibular ligament.

descriptionProfessional: The largest tarsal bone, forming the heel. The Achilles tendon inserts on its back and it bears the weight at heel strike.
descriptionPatient: Your heel bone. It is the largest bone in your foot and takes the impact when you walk.
apBiologyFacts: It is the attachment for the Achilles tendon, the strongest tendon in the body, from gastrocnemius and soleus, which plantarflexes the foot for push-off.
It forms the hind end of the longitudinal arch and absorbs the shock of heel strike.
It has a thin cortex and mainly spongy bone that makes it prone to crushing.
clinicalNotes: A fall from a height can fracture the calcaneus, often bilaterally; the spine should be checked at the same time because the force travels up the legs.
Plantar fasciitis, inflammation of the ligament under the foot at its heel attachment, is the leading cause of heel pain, and sometimes goes with a bony heel spur.
Haglund deformity is a bony bump at the back of the heel that irritates the Achilles.

descriptionProfessional: The navicular, cuboid and three cuneiform bones of the midfoot, which with the talus and calcaneus make the seven tarsals and form the arches of the foot.
descriptionPatient: The small bones in the middle of your foot that form its arch.
apBiologyFacts: The tarsals are held by ligaments in three arches - medial and lateral longitudinal, and transverse - that act like springs, storing energy as the foot lands and returning it in push-off.
Seven tarsals in the foot correspond to the eight carpals in the hand, showing the foot and hand as homologous structures adapted to different functions.
Human feet have a fixed, non-opposable big toe, an adaptation for bipedal walking.
clinicalNotes: Stress fractures of the navicular occur in runners and jumpers and are easy to miss.
Flat feet (pes planus) result when the medial arch collapses.
Lisfranc injuries disrupt the joints between the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases.

descriptionProfessional: Five long bones forming the forefoot, numbered I-V from the big toe. Their heads form the ball of the foot; the first is the stoutest.
descriptionPatient: The five long bones in the front part of your foot, ending in the ball of your foot.
apBiologyFacts: The first metatarsal is the stoutest because the big toe bears the push-off in walking and running; the heads of the metatarsals spread the load across the ball of the foot.
Together with the phalanges they form the forefoot; bones and ligaments make the arch that gives the human foot its springy stride.
clinicalNotes: A Jones fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal heals poorly because of a limited blood supply.
A 'march fracture' is a stress fracture of the second or third metatarsal from repetitive walking or running.
A bunion (hallux valgus) is a bony bump at the base of the big toe with the toe angled outwards.

descriptionProfessional: Fourteen bones in each foot: two in the big toe and three in each of the other four toes.
descriptionPatient: The bones of your toes - two in the big toe and three in each of the others.
apBiologyFacts: The big toe has two phalanges, the others three, and the toes are much shorter than the fingers because they are used for balance and push-off, not for grasping.
The big toe (hallux) has lost its opposability compared with other apes: an evolutionary change tied to upright walking.
The toes help balance: the pressure under them adjusts constantly to keep you upright.
clinicalNotes: Gout classically attacks the joint at the base of the big toe (podagra), when uric acid crystals deposit there.
Turf toe is a sprain of the big toe's base joint from hyperextension; hammer toe is a deformity where the middle joint is fixed in flexion.
Diabetic patients with neuropathy can develop toe ulcers and infection without feeling them.

descriptionProfessional: A thin triangular muscle deep to pectoralis major, from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid process of the scapula. It draws the scapula forward and down, and lifts the ribs in forced inspiration.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle under your big chest muscle that pulls your shoulder blade forward and down.
apBiologyFacts: It is an accessory muscle of inspiration: with the scapula fixed, it lifts ribs 3-5 to enlarge the chest, which is why people with severe asthma brace their arms and shoulders to breathe.
It lies over the axillary artery and the cords of the brachial plexus, so its tightness can compress them.
It is supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5-T1).
clinicalNotes: Pectoralis minor syndrome, a form of thoracic outlet syndrome, causes arm pain and numbness when the tight muscle presses on the neurovascular bundle.
It is a landmark for dividing the axillary artery into three parts.

descriptionProfessional: Two flat muscles from the spinous processes of C7-T5 to the medial border of the scapula, retracting it toward the spine and holding it against the chest wall.
descriptionPatient: Muscles between your shoulder blades that pull them together, like squeezing a pencil between them.
apBiologyFacts: Antagonistic pairs let joints move both ways: the rhomboids retract the scapula (pull it toward the spine) while serratus anterior protracts it - the classic push-pull pairing.
They are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5).
They hold the scapula flat against the ribs, so weakness makes its medial edge stick out.
clinicalNotes: Damage to the dorsal scapular nerve or muscle weakness leads to scapular 'winging' toward the spine side.
Sore, knotted rhomboids are a common source of upper-back pain in people who sit hunched at a desk.

descriptionProfessional: A strap from the transverse processes of C1-C4 to the upper medial border of the scapula, elevating the scapula and helping to tilt the neck to the same side.
descriptionPatient: The muscle that lifts your shoulder blade when you shrug and helps tilt your neck.
apBiologyFacts: Named for its action: it 'levates' (lifts) the scapula, as in shrugging.
Working from the neck downward with the scapula fixed, it bends the neck to the same side.
It is supplied by branches of C3-C4 and the dorsal scapular nerve.
clinicalNotes: It is a common site of neck and shoulder tension, giving the 'crick in the neck' after sleeping awkwardly.
Overuse from carrying heavy bags or working at a computer causes chronic trigger points.

descriptionProfessional: A rotator cuff muscle running from the supraspinous fossa of the scapula under the acromion to the greater tubercle of the humerus. It starts abduction of the arm and steadies the humeral head.
descriptionPatient: A small shoulder muscle that helps you start lifting your arm out to the side.
apBiologyFacts: It initiates the first 15 degrees of arm abduction, after which the deltoid takes over.

The four rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis - 'SITS') hold the ball of the humerus in the shallow glenoid socket, giving the shoulder its huge mobility at the cost of stability.
It is supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6).
clinicalNotes: It is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle, because its tendon passes through the narrow space beneath the acromion (impingement).
The 'empty can' test (arm raised with thumb down against resistance) reveals a tear or nerve palsy.

descriptionProfessional: A rotator cuff muscle filling the infraspinous fossa of the scapula and inserting on the greater tubercle. It is the chief external (lateral) rotator of the arm.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the back of your shoulder blade that turns your arm outward.
apBiologyFacts: Lateral rotation - turning the arm so the palm faces forward - depends mainly on this muscle; it is antagonised by subscapularis, the medial rotator.
It is supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6).
Together with the other cuff muscles it pulls the humeral head into the glenoid, which is why the joint stays in place during movement.
clinicalNotes: Rotator cuff tears involving infraspinatus weaken external rotation, so patients cannot comb the back of the hair or throw well.
Wasting of the infraspinatus fossa is seen after suprascapular nerve injury.

descriptionProfessional: The smallest rotator cuff muscle, from the lateral border of the scapula to the greater tubercle. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in the socket.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle at the back of the shoulder that helps turn your arm outward.
apBiologyFacts: It is the fourth rotator cuff muscle and works with infraspinatus for lateral rotation.
It is supplied by the axillary nerve, the same nerve that supplies the deltoid.
Together the cuff muscles are 'dynamic stabilisers' of a joint that has almost no bony stability.
clinicalNotes: Injury to the axillary nerve (for example in a shoulder dislocation) weakens both the deltoid and teres minor and causes numbness over the 'regimental badge' area of the upper arm.
Its tendon is rarely torn in isolation.

descriptionProfessional: A thick muscle from the lower lateral border of the scapula to the front of the humerus, adducting and medially rotating the arm; often called 'the lat's little helper'.
descriptionPatient: A muscle behind your armpit that pulls your arm down and turns it inward.
apBiologyFacts: It works with latissimus dorsi to extend, adduct and medially rotate the arm, as in pulling down a rope.
It is not part of the rotator cuff, although it lies right beside it.
It is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve (C5-C7).
clinicalNotes: It forms the lower border of the 'quadrangular space', through which the axillary nerve passes; entrapment there causes shoulder pain and weakness.
It is often tender in swimmers and rowers.

descriptionProfessional: The largest rotator cuff muscle, filling the front (costal surface) of the scapula and inserting on the lesser tubercle. It medially rotates the arm and stabilises the joint from the front.
descriptionPatient: A big muscle on the underside of your shoulder blade that turns your arm inward.
apBiologyFacts: It is the internal (medial) rotator of the cuff, opposing infraspinatus and teres minor.
It lies between the scapula and the rib cage, which is why it is the only cuff muscle you cannot see from behind.
It is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.
clinicalNotes: It stabilises the front of the shoulder, so tears are associated with anterior instability and dislocation.
The 'lift-off test' (hand behind the back, lifting away from the spine) tests it.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle lying deep to biceps on the front of the humerus, inserting on the ulna. It is the main flexor of the elbow, acting whatever position the forearm is in.
descriptionPatient: A muscle under your biceps that does most of the work of bending your elbow.
apBiologyFacts: It is the 'workhorse' of elbow flexion because it acts on the ulna, which does not rotate, so it works in pronation and supination alike.
Biceps is a stronger flexor when the forearm is supinated, but brachialis contributes equally in any position.
It is supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve, with a small part of the radial nerve.
clinicalNotes: It is at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, and a fibrosed brachialis can restrict elbow movement.
A biceps tendon rupture leaves elbow flexion largely intact because brachialis compensates.

descriptionProfessional: A slim muscle from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus, flexing and adducting the arm. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle in your upper arm that helps swing your arm forward and toward your body.
apBiologyFacts: It is the landmark for the axillary artery, which runs along its edge.
The musculocutaneous nerve passes through it, and the nerve supplies all three muscles of the anterior arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis).
It flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
clinicalNotes: Compression of the musculocutaneous nerve where it pierces the muscle causes weakness of elbow flexion and numbness along the outer forearm.
It is an anatomical landmark used in shoulder surgery.

descriptionProfessional: A long muscle from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the styloid process of the radius. It flexes the elbow, especially with the forearm in mid-pronation, as when hammering or drinking from a cup.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the outer side of your forearm that helps bend your elbow when your thumb points up.
apBiologyFacts: It is unusual: it lies in the extensor (back) compartment of the forearm but flexes the elbow, and is supplied by the radial nerve, showing that function does not always follow compartment.
It works best in the neutral 'handshake' position, where it is a strong elbow flexor.
Its tendon inserts at the far end of the radius, giving a long lever.
clinicalNotes: The brachioradialis reflex (tapping the radius above the wrist) tests the C5-C6 spinal segments.
It is a landmark for finding the radial artery and the superficial radial nerve.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle from the medial epicondyle of the humerus to the middle of the radius, rotating the forearm so the palm faces down (pronation) and helping to flex the elbow.
descriptionPatient: A muscle that turns your palm to face down.
apBiologyFacts: Pronation happens when the radius crosses over the ulna, driven by pronator teres above and pronator quadratus at the wrist.
The median nerve passes between the muscle's two heads.
It is the antagonist of supinator and biceps, which turn the palm up.
clinicalNotes: Pronator syndrome is compression of the median nerve where it passes between the heads, causing forearm pain and numbness in the hand like carpal tunnel syndrome.
It is a common site of pain in golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis).

descriptionProfessional: A forearm flexor from the medial epicondyle to the base of the second and third metacarpals, flexing and abducting the wrist. Its tendon is a landmark just beside the radial pulse.
descriptionPatient: A wrist muscle on the thumb side that bends your wrist and tilts it toward your thumb.
apBiologyFacts: Wrist flexors work in pairs to bend the wrist straight, and with the extensors to tilt it sideways (deviation).
Its tendon lies in front of the wrist, just medial to the radial artery, and is a guide for finding the pulse.
It is supplied by the median nerve (C6-C7).
clinicalNotes: Medial epicondylitis ('golfer's elbow') affects the common flexor origin at the elbow.
The tendon is a landmark in carpal tunnel release surgery.

descriptionProfessional: A slender muscle with a long tendon from the medial epicondyle to the palmar aponeurosis. About 14% of people lack it on one or both sides; it is a weak wrist flexor.
descriptionPatient: A thin muscle in the middle of your forearm that some people do not have at all.
apBiologyFacts: It is a vestigial muscle: it is strong in animals that walk on their hands, and absent in some people with no functional loss - evidence of evolutionary change in the human forelimb.
You can test for it by touching your thumb to your little finger and flexing the wrist; a tendon stands up in the centre of the wrist if present.
It is supplied by the median nerve.
clinicalNotes: Surgeons use its tendon as a graft to reconstruct other tendons, because it can be removed without loss of function.
It lies over the median nerve at the wrist, so it is a surface landmark for it.

descriptionProfessional: The largest superficial forearm flexor. Its four tendons split at the fingers to let the deeper flexor pass through, and it flexes the middle phalanx of each finger.
descriptionPatient: The big muscle in your forearm that curls your fingers into a fist.
apBiologyFacts: Its tendons pass through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve, alongside the deep flexors, and each splits to let the deep tendon travel to the fingertip.
It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints; flexor digitorum profundus flexes the fingertip joints.
It is supplied by the median nerve.
clinicalNotes: Tendon injuries in the palm are among the most difficult hand injuries to repair because the tendons run in tight sheaths.
Flexor tenosynovitis ('trigger finger' is one form) causes a finger to lock in flexion.

descriptionProfessional: The most medial forearm flexor, from the medial epicondyle and olecranon to the pisiform, hamate and fifth metacarpal. It flexes and adducts the wrist, and the ulnar nerve runs beneath it.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the little-finger side of your forearm that bends your wrist toward your pinky.
apBiologyFacts: It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, which enters the forearm between its two heads - the cubital tunnel.
It inserts on the pisiform, the only carpal bone that acts like a sesamoid inside a tendon.
Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris together adduct (ulnar deviate) the wrist.
clinicalNotes: Cubital tunnel syndrome, compression of the ulnar nerve here, causes tingling in the little and ring fingers.
Its tendon is a landmark for the ulnar artery and nerve at the wrist.

descriptionProfessional: Two muscles from the lateral epicondyle and supracondylar ridge to the bases of the second and third metacarpals, extending and abducting the wrist. The brevis is the more heavily used.
descriptionPatient: The muscles on the back of your forearm that lift your wrist and keep it steady when you grip.
apBiologyFacts: They stabilise the wrist in extension so the finger flexors can grip forcefully - which is why grip strength is weakest when the wrist is flexed.
They are supplied by the radial nerve.
Together with the flexor carpi radialis they tilt the wrist toward the thumb.
clinicalNotes: Lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow') is degeneration at the common extensor origin, especially the brevis tendon, from repeated wrist extension.
Radial nerve palsy causes 'wrist drop' because these muscles cannot extend the wrist.

descriptionProfessional: The main extensor of the four fingers, from the lateral epicondyle to the extensor expansions on the back of the fingers, joined by junctions on the back of the hand.
descriptionPatient: The muscle on the back of your forearm that straightens your fingers.
apBiologyFacts: Fingers are opened by extensors on the back of the forearm and closed by flexors on the front, supplied by different nerves - radial versus median and ulnar.
The four tendons on the back of the hand are linked by intertendinous connections, which is why it is hard to lift the ring finger alone.
It is supplied by the posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve.
clinicalNotes: Injury to the deep branch of the radial nerve causes 'finger drop' with the wrist still extending.
Ruptured extensor tendons in rheumatoid arthritis can suddenly prevent fingers straightening.

descriptionProfessional: A medial extensor of the forearm, from the lateral epicondyle and ulna to the base of the fifth metacarpal, extending and adducting the wrist.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the back of your forearm that bends your wrist backward and toward your pinky.
apBiologyFacts: With flexor carpi ulnaris it produces ulnar deviation of the wrist, as when you hammer.
It runs in a groove in the ulna's head and is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
It is the smallest of the wrist extensors that crosses the wrist at the ulnar side.
clinicalNotes: ECU tendinopathy and subluxation are common causes of ulnar-sided wrist pain in racquet-sport players.
Its tendon is a landmark to the ulnar styloid.

descriptionProfessional: The muscle group forming the fleshy base of the thumb: abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis, which oppose the thumb to the fingers.
descriptionPatient: The fleshy pad at the base of your thumb, which lets you pinch and grip.
apBiologyFacts: Opposition, bringing the thumb pad to meet the fingertips, depends on these muscles and is a key primate adaptation for precise manipulation.
They are supplied by the median nerve (recurrent branch), apart from part of flexor pollicis brevis.
The pad's size reflects how heavily the thumb is used.
clinicalNotes: Thenar wasting - a flattened thumb base - is a sign of severe or long-standing carpal tunnel syndrome.
Median nerve injury at the wrist abolishes thumb opposition, giving an 'ape hand'.

descriptionProfessional: The fleshy pad at the base of the little finger: abductor, flexor and opponens digiti minimi, moving and cupping the little finger.
descriptionPatient: The pad on the pinky side of your palm that helps you grip and cup your hand.
apBiologyFacts: These muscles cup the palm and help the little finger oppose the thumb.
They are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
Along with the thenar pad they define the shape of the palm.
clinicalNotes: Hypothenar wasting suggests ulnar nerve injury.
Repetitive impact to the base of the palm (hammering) can damage the ulnar artery at the hook of hamate (hypothenar hammer syndrome).

descriptionProfessional: The middle flank muscle, deep to the external oblique, with fibres running up and forward at right angles to it. It flexes and rotates the trunk and compresses the abdomen.
descriptionPatient: A muscle in the side of your belly, under the outer one, that helps you twist and bend.
apBiologyFacts: The three flat muscles of the abdominal wall (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus) have fibres running in different directions, like plywood, which makes the wall strong.
It works with the opposite-side external oblique to rotate the trunk, as when you twist to look behind you.
It is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves and the first lumbar nerve.
clinicalNotes: The abdominal wall's layered structure matters in surgery: incisions are made to split fibres where possible rather than cut them.
Inguinal hernias arise through a weak point where the layers are thinnest, the inguinal canal.

descriptionProfessional: The deepest flat muscle of the abdominal wall, with fibres running horizontally like a corset. It compresses the abdomen and stabilises the spine.
descriptionPatient: The deepest belly muscle, which wraps around your middle like a natural corset.
apBiologyFacts: It is the body's 'corset': contracting it draws in the abdominal wall and raises pressure inside the abdomen, which helps in coughing, defecation, childbirth and stabilising the lower spine.
It is the first abdominal muscle to activate before a limb movement, protecting the back.
It is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves and the first lumbar nerve.
clinicalNotes: Weakness is associated with low back pain, so 'core' exercises target it.
It forms the deepest layer of the rectus sheath and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

descriptionProfessional: A deep muscle of the posterior abdominal wall from the 12th rib and lumbar vertebrae to the iliac crest, bending the trunk sideways and fixing the 12th rib in breathing.
descriptionPatient: A deep muscle in your lower back that helps you bend sideways and hold your posture.
apBiologyFacts: It laterally flexes the spine, and when both sides contract it extends it.
It anchors the 12th rib during breathing so the diaphragm can pull against it.
It lies just behind the kidneys.
clinicalNotes: It is a common source of low back pain, especially after lifting with a twist.
The kidney sits on its anterior surface, so pain here can be confused with kidney disease.

descriptionProfessional: A long muscle from the lumbar vertebrae running through the pelvis to the lesser trochanter of the femur. With iliacus it is the strongest flexor of the hip and the only muscle attaching the spine to the leg.
descriptionPatient: A deep muscle from your lower spine to your thigh bone that lifts your knee when you walk.
apBiologyFacts: It is the only muscle connecting the trunk to the lower limb, so it helps keep the trunk upright over the legs.
Together with iliacus it forms the iliopsoas, the main hip flexor.
It is supplied by the anterior rami of L1-L3.
clinicalNotes: Psoas abscess, a deep infection tracking down the muscle, can present as pain in the groin and hip.
The 'psoas sign' (pain on extending the hip) can point to an inflamed appendix lying against it.

descriptionProfessional: A fan-shaped muscle filling the iliac fossa of the pelvis, joining psoas major to insert on the lesser trochanter. It flexes the hip.
descriptionPatient: A muscle lining the inside of your hip bone that helps you lift your leg forward.
apBiologyFacts: It lines the iliac fossa and joins psoas major in a common tendon - the iliopsoas.
The femoral nerve runs in the groove between the two muscles.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4).
clinicalNotes: An iliacus haematoma from a bleeding disorder or anticoagulation can compress the femoral nerve and cause thigh weakness and numbness.
Tight hip flexors contribute to lower back pain and an exaggerated lumbar curve.

descriptionProfessional: Three paired muscles from the cervical spine to the first and second ribs. They raise the upper ribs in breathing and bend the neck. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between two of them.
descriptionPatient: Muscles at the side of your neck that help you breathe in and tilt your head.
apBiologyFacts: They are accessory muscles of inspiration: they raise the first two ribs, which helps enlarge the upper chest, especially when breathing is laboured.
The brachial plexus roots and the subclavian artery emerge through the gap between scalenus anterior and medius.
They are supplied by the anterior rami of the cervical nerves.
clinicalNotes: Compression in the scalene triangle is one cause of thoracic outlet syndrome, causing arm pain, numbness and colour change.
The phrenic nerve runs on the front of scalenus anterior - a landmark for nerve blocks.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle with two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon anchored to the hyoid. It opens the mouth and raises the hyoid in swallowing.
descriptionPatient: A muscle under your jaw with two parts that helps you open your mouth and swallow.
apBiologyFacts: 'Digastric' means two bellies. The two bellies have different embryological origins and nerve supplies: the anterior belly by the trigeminal (from the first pharyngeal arch), the posterior belly by the facial nerve (from the second arch).
It depresses the mandible against gravity, opening the mouth, while the muscles of mastication close it.
The intermediate tendon slides through a fibrous sling attached to the hyoid.
clinicalNotes: Its posterior belly is a surgical landmark of the neck, marking the top of the carotid triangle.
It helps move the hyoid during swallowing; disorders of swallowing (dysphagia) can involve these suprahyoid muscles.

descriptionProfessional: A small muscle deep to the brow, drawing the eyebrows together and downward to make vertical frown lines.
descriptionPatient: The little muscle that pulls your eyebrows together when you frown.
apBiologyFacts: Facial expressions of emotion are produced by muscles that pull the skin: this one produces the frown of concentration or displeasure.
All muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
It creates the vertical 'eleven' lines between the eyebrows.
clinicalNotes: Botulinum toxin injected into corrugator and procerus softens frown lines.
Facial nerve palsy weakens its action on the affected side.

descriptionProfessional: A small pyramidal muscle over the bridge of the nose which pulls the skin between the eyebrows downward, wrinkling the bridge of the nose.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle on the bridge of your nose that wrinkles it when you scowl.
apBiologyFacts: It is supplied by the facial nerve and forms horizontal wrinkles across the bridge of the nose.
It is a continuation of the frontalis muscle over the nasal bone, showing how muscles of expression form continuous sheets.
clinicalNotes: It is treated with botulinum toxin along with corrugator to reduce a scowl.
It is included in flap design in nose surgery.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle of the nose with a transverse part that compresses the nostrils and an alar part that flares them.
descriptionPatient: The muscle that flares your nostrils.
apBiologyFacts: Flaring the nostrils increases airflow during heavy breathing.
It is supplied by the facial nerve.
The nostrils are supported by cartilage; the muscle acts on the skin over them.
clinicalNotes: Nasal flaring in an infant is a sign of respiratory distress.
Facial nerve palsy can cause collapse of the nostril on the affected side during inspiration.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle from the maxilla below the eye socket to the skin of the upper lip, raising it, as in a sneer.
