descriptionPatient: The muscle that lifts your upper lip.
apBiologyFacts: It is supplied by the facial nerve and is one of the radiating muscles that move the lips.
It is the muscle that produces the expression of disgust or a sneer.
It lies just over the infraorbital foramen where the infraorbital nerve emerges.
clinicalNotes: Facial paralysis makes the upper lip droop on one side.
It is a landmark in cosmetic filler injection of the nasolabial fold.

descriptionProfessional: A triangular muscle from the mandible to the corner of the mouth, pulling the mouth down in a frown or expression of sadness.
descriptionPatient: The muscle that pulls the corners of your mouth down when you look sad.
apBiologyFacts: It is the antagonist of zygomaticus major, which lifts the corner of the mouth: together they set the mouth's expression.
It is supplied by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve.
The marginal mandibular branch runs along the jaw, where it is vulnerable to injury.
clinicalNotes: Injury to the marginal mandibular nerve, for example during surgery on the neck or jaw, causes an asymmetric smile.
It is treated with botulinum toxin for a downturned mouth.

descriptionProfessional: A small muscle at the tip of the chin that raises and wrinkles the chin skin and pushes the lower lip up, as in pouting.
descriptionPatient: The small muscle in your chin that makes it wrinkle when you pout.
apBiologyFacts: It is the muscle that dimples the chin skin when you pout or show doubt.
It is supplied by the facial nerve.
It arises from the mandible below the incisors and inserts in the skin of the chin.
clinicalNotes: An overactive mentalis causes a 'pebbled' chin and can be treated with botulinum toxin.
It is affected in surgical procedures on the chin.

descriptionProfessional: The largest muscle in the body and the main extensor of the hip, from the sacrum and back of the ilium to the femur and the iliotibial tract. It powers climbing, running and rising from a chair.
descriptionPatient: The big muscle of your buttock, which powers you when you climb stairs, run or stand up.
apBiologyFacts: It is the largest muscle in the body, an adaptation for upright walking and running: it hardly works in level walking but is powerful in climbing and sprinting.
It extends and laterally rotates the thigh, and through the iliotibial tract helps stabilise the knee.
It is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2).
clinicalNotes: Injections into the buttock are given in the upper outer quadrant to avoid the sciatic nerve, which runs beneath.
Weakness of the muscle makes it hard to climb stairs or rise from sitting, and causes a backward lurch in walking.
Pressure ulcers commonly form over the sitting bones where gluteus maximus does not cushion.

descriptionProfessional: A fan-shaped muscle on the outer surface of the ilium inserting on the greater trochanter. It abducts the thigh and, in walking, holds the pelvis level when the opposite foot is lifted.
descriptionPatient: A muscle at the side of your hip that keeps your pelvis level as you walk.
apBiologyFacts: When you stand on one leg, gluteus medius on that side contracts to stop the pelvis from dropping on the other side.
It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1).
Together with gluteus minimus it abducts and medially rotates the thigh.
clinicalNotes: The Trendelenburg sign - the pelvis dropping on the unsupported side when standing on one leg - indicates weakness of gluteus medius or damage to the superior gluteal nerve.
Weakness produces a waddling gait, as in some hip disorders.

descriptionProfessional: A pear-shaped muscle from the front of the sacrum to the greater trochanter, laterally rotating the hip. The sciatic nerve passes near or through it.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle deep in your buttock that turns your leg outward.
apBiologyFacts: It is a landmark of the gluteal region: the nerves and vessels leave the pelvis above and below it.
The sciatic nerve usually emerges below it, but in some people it passes through or above it.
It is supplied by branches of S1-S2.
clinicalNotes: Piriformis syndrome is irritation of the sciatic nerve by the muscle, causing buttock pain and sciatica-like symptoms.
It is easily confused with a herniated disc, so both are considered in sciatica.

descriptionProfessional: A small muscle from the front of the iliac crest that tenses the iliotibial tract, helping to abduct and flex the hip and steady the knee.
descriptionPatient: A small muscle at the front and side of your hip that steadies your knee.
apBiologyFacts: It tenses the iliotibial tract, a band of fascia along the outside of the thigh, which acts like a tie-rod stabilising the knee.
It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
It works with gluteus medius in walking.
clinicalNotes: A tight tensor fasciae latae and iliotibial band cause 'runner's knee' (iliotibial band syndrome) with pain on the outer knee.
It is used as a muscle flap in reconstructive surgery.

descriptionProfessional: A thick band of fascia along the outside of the thigh from the iliac crest to the lateral tibia, into which tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus insert.
descriptionPatient: A strong band of tissue along the outside of your thigh that helps keep your knee stable.
apBiologyFacts: It is connective tissue, not muscle: dense fibrous tissue rich in collagen that transmits force and stabilises the hip and knee.
Because it crosses both joints, it helps hold the pelvis and knee steady during standing and walking.
It is tensed by tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus.
clinicalNotes: Iliotibial band syndrome, friction where it slides over the lateral femoral condyle, is a leading cause of lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists.
A section of the tract is sometimes used in knee ligament reconstruction.

descriptionProfessional: The only head of the quadriceps that crosses the hip as well as the knee, arising from the anterior inferior iliac spine. It flexes the hip and extends the knee.
descriptionPatient: The middle muscle at the front of your thigh, which lifts your knee and straightens your leg.
apBiologyFacts: The quadriceps is the largest muscle mass of the body, with four heads that share one tendon around the patella - the strongest extensor of the knee.
Rectus femoris crosses two joints, so it flexes the hip and extends the knee, which is why kicking a ball uses both actions.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4).
clinicalNotes: The knee-jerk (patellar) reflex tests the femoral nerve and the L3-L4 segments.
Rectus femoris strain is a common injury in sprinters and kickers.
Quadriceps wasting quickly follows knee injuries and is a focus of rehabilitation.

descriptionProfessional: The largest head of the quadriceps, on the outside of the thigh, from the greater trochanter and linea aspera to the patella. It extends the knee.
descriptionPatient: The biggest of the four front-of-thigh muscles, on the outside of your thigh.
apBiologyFacts: It is the largest of the quadriceps heads and a prime mover in extending the knee, as in standing up or climbing.
All four quadriceps heads join at the quadriceps tendon, enclosing the patella, which acts as a pulley increasing the muscle's leverage.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinicalNotes: It is a favoured site for intramuscular injections in infants because it is large and away from major nerves and vessels.
Muscle biopsies for diagnosing muscle disease are often taken from it.

descriptionProfessional: The medial head of the quadriceps, whose lowest fibres (vastus medialis obliquus) pull the patella inward and prevent it dislocating outward.
descriptionPatient: The teardrop-shaped muscle on the inner side of your knee that keeps your kneecap in place.
apBiologyFacts: Its low, oblique fibres counter the outward pull of the quadriceps on the patella, keeping it tracking in its groove.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve.
It forms the bulge just above the inner knee.
clinicalNotes: Weakness of vastus medialis is linked to patellofemoral pain and to the patella slipping outward.
It wastes rapidly after knee injury, so strengthening it is central to knee rehabilitation.

descriptionProfessional: The deep head of the quadriceps lying on the front of the femur beneath rectus femoris, extending the knee.
descriptionPatient: The deepest of the four front-of-thigh muscles, lying right on your thigh bone.
apBiologyFacts: It lies directly on the femur, beneath rectus femoris, and cannot be seen without removing that muscle.
It works with the other quadriceps heads to straighten the knee.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinicalNotes: Femoral shaft fractures can injure it, and scarring can limit knee flexion (quadriceps contracture).
It is sometimes grouped with the other three as the 'quads' in clinical tests.

descriptionProfessional: The continuation of the quadriceps tendon from the lower pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity, transmitting the quadriceps' force to extend the knee. Technically a ligament, since it joins bone to bone.
descriptionPatient: The strong cord below your kneecap that connects it to your shin bone.
apBiologyFacts: It links the quadriceps, through the patella, to the tibia. Because it connects two bones it is called a ligament, though it is the tendon's continuation.
The patella is a sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon, and increases its leverage.
Tapping this tendon produces the knee-jerk reflex, a monosynaptic stretch reflex.
clinicalNotes: Patellar tendinitis ('jumper's knee') is overuse pain at the lower pole of the patella in athletes.
A patellar tendon graft is one option for reconstructing the anterior cruciate ligament.
In Osgood-Schlatter disease, the tendon's pull irritates the growing tibial tuberosity in adolescents.

descriptionProfessional: The longest muscle in the body, a strap running from the anterior superior iliac spine obliquely across the thigh to the inner tibia. It flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee: the movement of sitting cross-legged.
descriptionPatient: The longest muscle in your body, a thin strap across your thigh that lets you sit cross-legged.
apBiologyFacts: It is the longest muscle in the body; its name comes from the Latin for tailor, who sat cross-legged.
It crosses both hip and knee and forms the roof of the adductor canal that carries the femoral artery.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinicalNotes: It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle, an important landmark in the groin.
Its insertion is one of the three tendons of the pes anserinus on the medial tibia.

descriptionProfessional: A slender muscle along the inner thigh from the pubis to the medial tibia, adducting the hip and flexing the knee.
descriptionPatient: A thin muscle along the inside of your thigh that pulls your leg toward the other.
apBiologyFacts: It is the only adductor to cross the knee, so it also flexes the knee.
It is supplied by the obturator nerve (L2-L3).
Its tendon forms part of the pes anserinus with sartorius and semitendinosus.
clinicalNotes: Gracilis is a common donor muscle for reconstructive surgery, as it can be removed without noticeable loss of function.
It is often strained in sports needing sudden changes of direction, such as football.

descriptionProfessional: The most anterior of the adductors, from the pubis to the middle of the femur, adducting the thigh. It forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.
descriptionPatient: A muscle in your groin and inner thigh that pulls your leg inward.
apBiologyFacts: Adductors pull the thigh toward the midline - the opposite action to gluteus medius and minimus.
It is supplied by the obturator nerve.
Its tendon is the most prominent one you can feel in the groin.
clinicalNotes: An adductor longus strain is a 'groin strain', common in footballers, ice-hockey players and sprinters.
It is a landmark for the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, where the femoral vessels and nerve lie.

descriptionProfessional: The largest adductor, with an adductor part (obturator nerve) and a hamstring part (sciatic nerve) - a muscle with a dual nerve supply and dual role.
descriptionPatient: The large muscle of your inner thigh that pulls your leg in and helps extend your hip.
apBiologyFacts: It has two parts with different nerve supplies - obturator for the adductor part, tibial division of the sciatic for the hamstring part - reflecting different embryological origins.
The adductor hiatus, the gap between its two parts near the knee, lets the femoral vessels pass to the back of the knee.
It adducts the thigh and helps to extend the hip.
clinicalNotes: Adductor group strains are common in athletes.
The adductor canal, beneath sartorius, is used for anaesthetic nerve blocks of the leg.

descriptionProfessional: The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischial tuberosity and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibular head. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.
descriptionPatient: The muscle on the outer back of your thigh that bends your knee.
apBiologyFacts: The hamstrings cross both hip and knee, extending the hip and flexing the knee - the muscles that propel you forward in running.
Its tendon forms the lateral border of the space behind the knee, and the common fibular nerve runs along it.
The long head is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve, the short head by the common fibular part.
clinicalNotes: Hamstring strains are among the commonest athletic injuries, usually at the junction of muscle and tendon in sprinters.
The common fibular nerve is at risk where the tendon passes by the fibular head.

descriptionProfessional: The superficial medial hamstring, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial tibia, with a long, cord-like tendon. It extends the hip and flexes and medially rotates the knee.
descriptionPatient: A hamstring muscle on the inner back of your thigh with a long, cord-like tendon.
apBiologyFacts: It is named for its long tendon - 'semi-tendinous' - which makes up the lower half of the muscle.
It is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.
Its tendon joins gracilis and sartorius at the pes anserinus.
clinicalNotes: Its tendon is commonly harvested to reconstruct the anterior cruciate ligament.
Hamstring tears often involve this muscle.

descriptionProfessional: The deeper medial hamstring, from the ischial tuberosity to the back of the medial tibial condyle, extending the hip and flexing and medially rotating the knee.
descriptionPatient: A hamstring muscle deep on the inner back of your thigh that bends your knee.
apBiologyFacts: It is named for the flat, membrane-like tendon at its upper end.
It is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.
It helps stabilise the back of the knee, pulling on the capsule as the knee bends.
clinicalNotes: A Baker's cyst forms where fluid bulges between semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius at the back of the knee.
Hamstring injuries may involve its proximal tendon.

descriptionProfessional: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body, joining the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus. It transmits the force that pushes the foot down in walking, running and jumping.
descriptionPatient: The thick cord at the back of your ankle that lets you push off the ground.
apBiologyFacts: It is the body's strongest tendon and can withstand loads several times body weight in running.
Tendons are dense regular connective tissue, mostly parallel collagen fibres, with few cells and a poor blood supply, so they heal slowly.
It is named for Achilles, the Greek hero whose only weak point was his heel.
clinicalNotes: It is the most commonly ruptured tendon in weekend athletes, with a sudden 'pop' and inability to rise onto the toes; the Thompson test (squeezing the calf) shows no foot movement.
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics increase the risk of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture.
The Achilles reflex tests the S1 nerve root.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle of the front of the leg with tendons to the four lesser toes. It extends the toes and dorsiflexes the ankle.
descriptionPatient: A muscle at the front of your shin that lifts your toes and foot.
apBiologyFacts: It lies in the anterior compartment of the leg, supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
It works with tibialis anterior to dorsiflex the ankle, lifting the front of the foot so the toes clear the ground in walking.
Its four tendons fan out over the top of the foot.
clinicalNotes: Deep fibular nerve injury causes weakness of dorsiflexion and toe extension, contributing to foot drop.
Anterior compartment syndrome, from swelling in a closed fascial space after trauma, threatens this muscle group and is a surgical emergency.

descriptionProfessional: A muscle of the lateral leg whose tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot to the first metatarsal. It everts the foot and helps support the arch.
descriptionPatient: A muscle on the outside of your lower leg that turns your foot outward and supports its arch.
apBiologyFacts: Eversion turns the sole outward; it opposes tibialis posterior, which inverts the foot.
The tendon runs under the sole like a stirrup, helping to support the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches.
It is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.
clinicalNotes: Ankle inversion sprains often stress the peroneal tendons, which can dislocate from their groove behind the malleolus.
Damage to the common fibular nerve weakens eversion as well as dorsiflexion.

descriptionProfessional: The deepest muscle of the calf, whose tendon passes behind the medial malleolus to the navicular and other tarsals. It inverts the foot and is the main support of the medial arch.
descriptionPatient: A deep calf muscle that turns your foot inward and holds up the arch of your foot.
apBiologyFacts: It is the chief dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot.
Its tendon is the most anterior of the structures behind the medial malleolus ('Tom, Dick and Harry': tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus).
It is supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinicalNotes: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flat foot in adults.
Medial tibial stress syndrome ('shin splints') involves its origin on the tibia.

descriptionProfessional: A deep muscle of the calf whose tendons pass under the foot to the four lesser toes, flexing them and helping to plantarflex the ankle.
descriptionPatient: A deep calf muscle that curls your toes downward.
apBiologyFacts: It flexes the toes, gripping the ground as you push off.
Its tendon runs behind the medial malleolus, then across the sole to the four lesser toes.
It is supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinicalNotes: Tarsal tunnel syndrome, compression of the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus, can involve its tendon.
Its tendon is transferred to correct some deformities of the toes and foot.

descriptionProfessional: The thick-walled left lower chamber that receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and ejects it into the aorta against systemic vascular resistance.
descriptionPatient: The main pumping chamber of your heart. It pushes oxygen-rich blood out to the rest of your body.
apBiologyFacts: Its wall is 10-15 mm thick versus 3-5 mm on the right, because systemic resistance is far higher than pulmonary resistance. Same stroke volume, much greater pressure.
The Frank-Starling relationship: greater venous return stretches the myocardium, improving actin-myosin overlap, so stroke volume rises to match preload automatically.
Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume; a healthy ventricle ejects 55-70% and never empties completely.
clinicalNotes: Chronic hypertension or aortic stenosis drives left ventricular hypertrophy - initially compensatory, eventually a cause of diastolic failure.
Heart failure is split into HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction, a pump problem) and HFpEF (preserved EF, a filling problem); the treatments differ substantially.
Echocardiography is the first-line test for chamber size, wall motion and ejection fraction.

descriptionProfessional: The posterior-most chamber, receiving oxygenated blood from four pulmonary veins and delivering it across the mitral valve.
descriptionPatient: The chamber that collects fresh, oxygen-rich blood coming back from your lungs.
apBiologyFacts: It receives blood from four pulmonary veins - the only veins in the body carrying oxygenated blood.
Most ventricular filling is passive; atrial contraction ('atrial kick') adds only the final 20-30%, which is why people can tolerate losing coordinated atrial contraction at rest.
clinicalNotes: Atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation, where disorganized electrical activity replaces coordinated contraction.
Stasis in the left atrial appendage during AF forms thrombi that embolize to the brain - this is why AF patients are anticoagulated.
Mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure and backs up into the pulmonary circulation, causing dyspnea.

descriptionProfessional: The thin-walled chamber that receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, then passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle. It contains the sinoatrial node.
descriptionPatient: The upper right chamber of your heart, where blood that has been all around your body arrives back.
apBiologyFacts: Blood returns to the heart in the right atrium: the venae cavae empty into it, and it pushes blood down through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
The sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's natural pacemaker, lies in its wall near the entrance of the superior vena cava and sets the heart rate.
Atria are low-pressure, thin-walled chambers; they act mainly as reservoirs and fill the ventricles, contributing about 20% of ventricular filling.
clinicalNotes: Atrial fibrillation, a chaotic rhythm of the atria, is the commonest sustained arrhythmia and raises stroke risk because blood pools and clots in the atrial appendage.
A raised jugular venous pressure reflects high right atrial pressure, an early sign of right heart failure.
Central venous catheters are threaded so that their tip lies at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium.

descriptionProfessional: The chamber forming most of the front of the heart. It receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery, to the lungs, against low resistance.
descriptionPatient: The lower right chamber of your heart, which pumps blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen.
apBiologyFacts: Its wall is only 3-5 mm thick, about a third of the left ventricle's, because the pulmonary circuit has much lower resistance than the systemic one.
It pumps the same stroke volume as the left ventricle at lower pressure (about 25 mmHg systolic against 120), so both sides move equal volumes per beat.
It is the most anterior chamber, lying directly behind the sternum.
clinicalNotes: Because it sits at the front, the right ventricle is the chamber most likely to be injured in a stab wound or blunt chest trauma.
Pulmonary hypertension or a large pulmonary embolus makes it work against higher pressure, so it dilates and fails (cor pulmonale).
The tetralogy of Fallot, a congenital defect, includes right ventricular outflow obstruction and a thickened right ventricle.

descriptionProfessional: The cartilaginous box at the top of the trachea, made of the shield-shaped thyroid cartilage, the ring-shaped cricoid and smaller cartilages. It houses the vocal cords and guards the airway during swallowing.
descriptionPatient: Your voice box, which makes sound when air passes over your vocal cords and shuts to keep food out of your windpipe.
apBiologyFacts: Sound is made when exhaled air makes the vocal folds vibrate; pitch depends on their tension and length, which is why male voices, with longer folds after puberty, are lower.
During swallowing the larynx rises and the epiglottis tips over its opening, directing food to the oesophagus rather than the airway.
The thyroid cartilage forms the 'Adam's apple', more prominent in males after puberty.
clinicalNotes: Choking is obstruction at or below the larynx; the Heimlich manoeuvre uses abdominal pressure to expel the object.
Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops under the aortic arch on the left, causes hoarseness - a reason thyroid surgery risks the voice.
The cricoid is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, the site of emergency cricothyroidotomy when the airway cannot be secured.

descriptionProfessional: The two airways into which the trachea divides at the carina, one to each lung. The right is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
descriptionPatient: The two large breathing tubes that split from your windpipe and carry air into each lung.
apBiologyFacts: The trachea divides at the carina at about the level of the sternal angle (T4-T5); each bronchus then divides repeatedly - lobar, segmental, then bronchioles - down to the alveoli, where gases are exchanged.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and steeper than the left, which is why inhaled objects, such as a swallowed peanut, more often lodge in the right lung.
Airways are lined by ciliated epithelium and mucus-secreting goblet cells that trap and sweep particles upward: the mucociliary escalator.
clinicalNotes: Smoking paralyses cilia and enlarges goblet cells, causing the chronic cough and mucus of chronic bronchitis.
Bronchoscopy passes a flexible camera into the bronchi to examine, biopsy or clear the airways.
Asthma narrows the airways by smooth muscle contraction, inflammation and mucus; bronchodilators such as salbutamol relax the muscle.

descriptionProfessional: The first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, curving around the head of the pancreas. It receives chyme from the stomach and bile and pancreatic juice through the ampulla of Vater.
descriptionPatient: The first part of your small intestine, where stomach contents mix with digestive juices from the liver and pancreas.
apBiologyFacts: Chyme from the stomach is acidic; the duodenum neutralises it with bicarbonate from the pancreas so that digestive enzymes, which work at neutral to slightly alkaline pH, can function.
Bile (made in the liver, stored in the gallbladder) emulsifies fats, and pancreatic enzymes - lipase, amylase and proteases - digest fats, carbohydrates and proteins.
Hormones from its wall control the process: secretin triggers bicarbonate release and cholecystokinin (CCK) triggers gallbladder contraction and enzyme secretion.
clinicalNotes: A duodenal ulcer, often caused by Helicobacter pylori, causes gnawing pain that eases with food; bleeding from it can be severe.
Coeliac disease flattens the villi of the duodenum and jejunum, causing malabsorption; it is diagnosed by biopsy of the duodenum.
Gallstones lodged at the ampulla can block both the bile and pancreatic ducts, causing jaundice and pancreatitis.

descriptionProfessional: The middle part of the small intestine, about 2.5 m long, where most nutrient absorption takes place. It has tall circular folds and dense villi, giving it a thick wall and deep colour.
descriptionPatient: The middle section of your small intestine, where most of the food you eat is absorbed into your blood.
apBiologyFacts: The small intestine's surface area (about 30 m2 for absorption) is greatly increased by three levels of folding: circular folds, finger-like villi, and microvilli on each cell (the brush border).
Each villus contains a capillary network, which takes up sugars and amino acids into the hepatic portal system, and a lacteal, a lymph vessel that carries absorbed fats.
Most absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat is complete by the end of the jejunum.
clinicalNotes: Short bowel syndrome, after extensive surgical removal of small intestine, leaves too little surface for absorption.
Crohn's disease can affect any part of the small intestine and causes inflammation, strictures and malabsorption.
Small bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, vomiting and abdominal distension, often from adhesions after surgery.

descriptionProfessional: The last part of the small intestine, about 3.5 m long, joining the caecum at the ileocaecal valve. It absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts and contains aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches).
descriptionPatient: The final section of your small intestine, which absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts before passing waste into the large intestine.
apBiologyFacts: The ileum specifically absorbs vitamin B12 (bound to intrinsic factor from the stomach) and recycles bile salts back to the liver in the enterohepatic circulation.
Peyer's patches - clusters of lymphoid tissue in its wall - sample bacteria and antigens, part of the gut's immune defences.
The ileocaecal valve prevents backflow from the large intestine, which has a heavy bacterial load.
clinicalNotes: Removal or disease of the terminal ileum (as in Crohn's disease) causes vitamin B12 deficiency and bile-salt malabsorption, leading to diarrhoea.
Meckel's diverticulum, a remnant of the embryonic yolk stalk, is found on the ileum in about 2% of people.
Right-sided lower abdominal pain can be from terminal ileitis as well as appendicitis.

descriptionProfessional: A blind-ended pouch at the start of the large intestine, in the right lower abdomen below the entry of the ileum. The appendix hangs from it.
descriptionPatient: The pouch at the start of your large intestine, where the small intestine empties in and where your appendix is attached.
apBiologyFacts: In herbivores the caecum is large and holds bacteria that ferment plant cellulose; in humans it is small, showing how the same organ is adapted differently by diet.
The ileocaecal valve controls flow from ileum to caecum and prevents backflow.
Fluid and salt absorption begins here, as the large intestine reclaims water from the remaining contents.
clinicalNotes: A caecal volvulus or a tumour of the caecum in older adults can cause obstruction or unexplained blood-loss anaemia.
Diverticular disease and caecal cancers are checked by colonoscopy.

descriptionProfessional: A narrow worm-shaped blind tube, about 9 cm long, projecting from the caecum. Its wall is rich in lymphoid tissue.
descriptionPatient: A small finger-shaped pouch attached to your large intestine, whose exact purpose is still debated.
apBiologyFacts: Long called vestigial, the appendix is now thought to act as a reservoir of beneficial gut bacteria that can repopulate the intestine after diarrhoeal illness, and its lymphoid tissue contributes to immune function.
Its narrow opening can be blocked by faecal matter or lymphoid swelling, trapping bacteria inside.
Comparing human anatomy with that of other primates and herbivores shows how organs can change function during evolution.
clinicalNotes: Appendicitis begins as vague pain around the navel, then localises to the right lower abdomen (McBurney's point) with fever and loss of appetite; untreated, it can perforate.
Appendectomy, usually laparoscopic, is one of the commonest emergency operations.
Rovsing's sign - pain in the right lower abdomen when the left is pressed - can point to appendicitis.

descriptionProfessional: The part of the large intestine that runs up the right side of the abdomen from the caecum to the hepatic flexure beneath the liver. It is retroperitoneal, fixed against the back wall.
descriptionPatient: The part of your large intestine that carries waste up the right side of your belly.
apBiologyFacts: The colon reabsorbs water and electrolytes, turning liquid chyme into formed faeces; most of the roughly 1.5 L of fluid entering the colon daily is reclaimed.
Bacteria in the colon ferment fibre, producing short-chain fatty acids that feed the colon's cells, and synthesise vitamin K and some B vitamins.
Bands of muscle (taeniae coli) puckering the wall produce its sacculations, the haustra.
clinicalNotes: Right-sided colon cancers often present with iron-deficiency anaemia from slow, occult bleeding rather than changes in bowel habit.
Colonoscopy screening from age 45 detects and removes polyps before they become malignant.

descriptionProfessional: The longest and most mobile part of the large intestine, crossing the abdomen from the hepatic to the splenic flexure, suspended by a mesentery and sagging below the stomach.
descriptionPatient: The section of your large intestine that crosses your belly from right to left.
apBiologyFacts: It is the only part of the colon suspended freely by a mesentery, so its position varies with posture and how full it is.
It marks the change between the midgut territory (supplied by the superior mesenteric artery) and hindgut (inferior mesenteric artery).
Haustral churning and mass movements push its contents onward, stimulated by eating (the gastrocolic reflex).
clinicalNotes: Toxic megacolon, a dangerous dilatation of the transverse colon, is a complication of severe ulcerative colitis.
The greater omentum hangs from it like an apron, and can wall off inflammation.

descriptionProfessional: The part of the large intestine that runs down the left side of the abdomen from the splenic flexure to the pelvis, where it becomes the sigmoid colon. It is retroperitoneal and narrower than the ascending colon.
descriptionPatient: The section of your large intestine that carries waste down the left side of your belly.
apBiologyFacts: Its contents are by now semi-solid; it mainly stores faeces before they move into the sigmoid colon and rectum.
It is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, the artery of the hindgut, and drained by the inferior mesenteric vein.
Its narrower lumen and more solid contents make obstruction here more likely.
clinicalNotes: Left-sided colon cancers often narrow the lumen and cause a change in bowel habit and visible blood in the stool.
Diverticulitis, inflamed outpouchings, is commonest in the descending and sigmoid colon and causes left lower abdominal pain.

descriptionProfessional: The S-shaped final part of the colon, in the pelvis, joining the descending colon to the rectum. It has a mesentery, so it is mobile.
descriptionPatient: The S-shaped part of your large intestine just before the rectum, where waste is stored until you go to the toilet.
apBiologyFacts: It stores formed faeces until defecation; its strong muscular contractions push contents into the rectum.
Stretching of the rectum triggers the defecation reflex, but the external anal sphincter is under voluntary control.
Its mobility means it can twist on its own mesentery.
clinicalNotes: Sigmoid volvulus - twisting of the loop - causes obstruction, most often in older, constipated adults, and appears as a 'coffee-bean' sign on X-ray.
It is the commonest site of diverticular disease and of colorectal cancer along with the rectum.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines it and the rectum.

descriptionProfessional: The final 12-15 cm of the large intestine, following the curve of the sacrum to the anal canal. It stores faeces and its stretching triggers the urge to defecate.
descriptionPatient: The last part of your large intestine, where waste waits until you are ready to pass it.
apBiologyFacts: The rectum stretches to hold faeces; filling triggers the defecation reflex, involving the parasympathetic pelvic nerves.
The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle, involuntary, while the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control via the pudendal nerve.
It follows the curve of the sacrum, having no haustra or taeniae in its lower part.
clinicalNotes: Colorectal cancer is the third commonest cancer worldwide; a digital rectal examination and screening find many early tumours.
Haemorrhoids are swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal, causing bright red bleeding.
Faecal incontinence can follow injury to the sphincters or the pudendal nerve, for example in childbirth.

descriptionProfessional: A muscular organ of the floor of the mouth, covered in papillae bearing taste buds. Its intrinsic and extrinsic muscles manipulate food and shape speech; the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies its movement.
descriptionPatient: The strong, flexible muscle in your mouth that helps you taste, chew, swallow and speak.
apBiologyFacts: Taste buds on the papillae detect five basic tastes - sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami - through receptor cells that bind chemicals dissolved in saliva.

Its movement is controlled by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); general sensation by the trigeminal (front two-thirds) and glossopharyngeal (back third); taste by the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves.
It begins mechanical digestion by pushing food into a bolus for swallowing, and saliva contains amylase that starts starch digestion.
clinicalNotes: When a patient sticks out the tongue and it deviates to one side, the hypoglossal nerve on that side is damaged.
A geographic or coated tongue is common; a persistent white or red patch may be a sign of cancer and should be examined.
Loss of taste (ageusia) can follow COVID-19, head injury or nerve damage.

descriptionProfessional: The largest salivary gland, lying in front of and below the ear over the masseter. It secretes watery, enzyme-rich saliva through the parotid duct into the mouth; the facial nerve runs through it.
descriptionPatient: The biggest of your saliva glands, in your cheek in front of your ear.
apBiologyFacts: Salivary glands secrete saliva containing water, mucus, salivary amylase (which starts the digestion of starch) and lysozyme (which attacks bacteria).
The three pairs of major glands are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual; the parotid makes mostly watery saliva.
Secretion is controlled by the autonomic nervous system: parasympathetic stimulation greatly increases watery saliva - the reason your mouth waters at the thought of food.
clinicalNotes: Mumps is a viral infection causing painful swelling of the parotid glands.
Because the facial nerve passes through the gland, surgery on it risks facial paralysis.
Stones in a salivary duct cause painful swelling during meals.

descriptionProfessional: A salivary gland below the body of the mandible, producing mixed serous and mucous saliva delivered into the floor of the mouth beside the tongue.
descriptionPatient: A saliva gland under your jaw, which keeps your mouth moist and helps you swallow.
apBiologyFacts: Produces about 70% of resting saliva; its mixed secretion moistens and lubricates food.
Saliva also buffers acid, protects teeth by delivering calcium and phosphate, and washes away bacteria.
It is supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the facial nerve.
clinicalNotes: Salivary stones (sialolithiasis) are commonest in this gland, causing pain and swelling under the jaw when eating.
Ranula is a cyst in the floor of the mouth from an obstructed sublingual gland.

descriptionProfessional: The largest lobe of the cerebral hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus. It contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area for speech production, and the prefrontal cortex for planning, judgement and personality.
descriptionPatient: The front part of your brain, which controls movement, planning, decisions and speaking.
apBiologyFacts: The primary motor cortex, in the precentral gyrus, sends commands to skeletal muscles; each part of the body has its own area, mapped in a distorted 'homunculus' with large areas for the hands and face.
Broca's area (usually in the left frontal lobe) produces speech; the prefrontal cortex handles planning, reasoning, impulse control and personality.

The cerebral cortex is folded into gyri and sulci, greatly increasing its surface area inside a skull of limited size; grey matter holds nerve cell bodies, white matter the myelinated tracts between them.
clinicalNotes: A stroke in the left frontal lobe can cause Broca's aphasia: speech is effortful and halting but comprehension is preserved; the right side of the body can be weak.
Frontal lobe injury, famously that of Phineas Gage, can change personality, judgement and impulse control.
Frontotemporal dementia begins with changes in behaviour or language.

descriptionProfessional: The lobe behind the central sulcus, containing the primary somatosensory cortex that receives touch, pain, temperature and body-position signals, and areas for spatial awareness and attention.
descriptionPatient: The top-back part of your brain, which processes touch and helps you know where your body is in space.
apBiologyFacts: The primary somatosensory cortex, in the postcentral gyrus, receives sensory information from the opposite side of the body, mapped as a sensory homunculus.
The parietal lobe integrates sensory information to give a sense of space, allowing you to reach for an object or navigate a room.
Sensory pathways cross (decussate), so the left hemisphere processes the right side of the body.
clinicalNotes: Damage to the right parietal lobe can cause hemispatial neglect: the patient ignores the left side of the body and world, even shaving only half the face.
Gerstmann syndrome, from left parietal damage, causes difficulty with writing, arithmetic, finger identification and left-right orientation.
Tests of two-point discrimination and stereognosis probe cortical sensation.

descriptionProfessional: The lobe below the lateral fissure, containing the primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area for language comprehension, and the hippocampus and amygdala involved in memory and emotion.
descriptionPatient: The part of your brain on the sides, near your ears, which handles hearing, understanding language and forming memories.
apBiologyFacts: The primary auditory cortex processes sound; Wernicke's area (usually left) is needed to understand spoken and written language.
The hippocampus, in the medial temporal lobe, is essential for forming new long-term (declarative) memories; the amygdala processes emotion, especially fear.
Memory formation involves long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of synapses that have been used together.
clinicalNotes: Alzheimer's disease begins in the medial temporal lobe, with loss of recent memory.
A stroke in Wernicke's area causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
Temporal lobe epilepsy can begin with a strange feeling of familiarity (déjà vu) or an odd smell, followed by loss of awareness.

descriptionProfessional: The smallest lobe, at the back of the hemisphere, containing the primary visual cortex that receives signals from the eyes via the optic radiations.
descriptionPatient: The back of your brain, which turns the signals from your eyes into the pictures you see.
apBiologyFacts: The primary visual cortex processes vision; the visual field is mapped upside down and reversed, and the left occipital lobe sees the right half of the visual field from both eyes.
Visual information travels from the retina through the optic nerve, chiasm, tract, thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) and optic radiations to this cortex.
Higher visual areas nearby recognise shapes, colours and motion.
clinicalNotes: A stroke of the occipital lobe causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia), often with the central vision spared.
Cortical blindness follows bilateral damage even though the eyes themselves are normal.
A visual aura before a migraine is generated in this lobe.

descriptionProfessional: The uppermost part of the brainstem, containing the nuclei for eye movement (CN III, IV), the substantia nigra, and pathways relaying visual and auditory reflexes.
descriptionPatient: The top part of your brainstem, which helps control eye movement and reflexes to sights and sounds.
apBiologyFacts: The substantia nigra produces dopamine and is central to movement control; its loss causes Parkinson's disease.
The superior colliculi coordinate visual reflexes and the inferior colliculi auditory reflexes.
The oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves arise here to move the eyes.
clinicalNotes: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra, causing tremor, rigidity and slowness of movement; levodopa replaces the dopamine.
A midbrain lesion can produce a fixed dilated pupil and an eye turned outward and down (CN III palsy).

descriptionProfessional: The bulging middle part of the brainstem, a bridge carrying signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum. It contains nuclei of cranial nerves V-VIII and centres that help regulate breathing.
descriptionPatient: The middle section of your brainstem, which relays messages between the two halves of your brain and helps control breathing and facial movement.
apBiologyFacts: 'Pons' means bridge: it carries fibres between the cortex and cerebellum, and pathways between brain and spinal cord.
It contains nuclei for the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves.
With the medulla, it helps regulate the rhythm of breathing.
clinicalNotes: A pontine stroke can cause 'locked-in syndrome': complete paralysis except for eye movements, with full awareness.
Central pontine myelinolysis follows overly rapid correction of low blood sodium.

descriptionProfessional: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. It contains vital centres for heart rate, blood pressure and breathing, and the nuclei for cranial nerves IX-XII.
descriptionPatient: The bottom of your brainstem, joining your brain to your spinal cord, which controls your heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing without your thinking about it.
apBiologyFacts: It houses the cardiovascular and respiratory centres: it detects rising CO2 (through changes in pH of the cerebrospinal fluid) and adjusts breathing rate to keep blood gases stable.
Most motor fibres cross (decussate) here in the pyramids, which is why each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.
Its centres also control reflexes such as vomiting, coughing, sneezing and swallowing.
clinicalNotes: Damage to the medulla, from a stroke or herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, can stop breathing and the heartbeat.
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome causes vertigo, difficulty swallowing and loss of pain and temperature sensation on one side of the face and the opposite side of the body.

descriptionProfessional: The eyeball: a fibrous outer coat (white sclera with a transparent cornea in front), a vascular middle coat with the iris, and a light-sensitive inner retina. The lens focuses light onto the retina, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.
descriptionPatient: Your eye, which focuses light onto a layer of cells that turn it into signals your brain sees as pictures.
apBiologyFacts: Light passes through the cornea (which does most of the focusing), the pupil, the lens and the vitreous humour to reach the retina, where rods (dim light, black and white) and cones (bright light, colour) transduce it into nerve impulses.
The iris controls pupil size: the sphincter pupillae constricts in bright light (parasympathetic) and the dilator pupillae widens it in dim light (sympathetic).
Accommodation: the ciliary muscle changes the lens's shape - relaxing to flatten it for distant objects and contracting to make it rounder for near ones.
clinicalNotes: Myopia (short-sightedness) focuses light in front of the retina and is corrected by a concave lens; hyperopia focuses it behind and is corrected by a convex lens.
Cataract is clouding of the lens; glaucoma is damage to the optic nerve, usually from raised pressure inside the eye.
The red reflex checked in newborns detects lens and retinal problems such as congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.

descriptionProfessional: Six muscles moving each eye: the superior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus, and the superior and inferior oblique. They are supplied by cranial nerves III, IV and VI.
descriptionPatient: The six small muscles around each eye that move it up, down and side to side.
apBiologyFacts: Nerve supply is remembered by 'LR6 SO4 the rest 3': the lateral rectus by the abducens (VI), the superior oblique by the trochlear (IV), the rest by the oculomotor (III).
The muscles work in antagonistic pairs and are coordinated so both eyes move together, keeping images on corresponding parts of each retina.
The superior oblique's tendon passes through a fibrous pulley (the trochlea) before inserting.
clinicalNotes: Damage to CN III gives a 'down and out' eye with a drooping lid and dilated pupil; to CN VI, an eye unable to look outward.
Strabismus (squint) is misalignment of the eyes; if untreated in childhood, the brain suppresses the image from one eye (amblyopia).
Entrapment of the inferior rectus in an orbital floor fracture causes double vision on looking up.

descriptionProfessional: The snail-shaped, fluid-filled spiral of the inner ear, about 2.5 turns long. Vibrations of the stapes move the fluid, bending hair cells on the basilar membrane that generate nerve impulses.
descriptionPatient: The spiral-shaped part of your inner ear that turns sound vibrations into nerve signals for your brain.
apBiologyFacts: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate; the three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify the vibration and pass it to the oval window, making the cochlear fluid move.
The basilar membrane is tuned along its length: high-pitched sounds vibrate its base, low-pitched sounds its apex, so pitch is encoded by which hair cells fire.
Hair cells' stereocilia bend, opening ion channels, and the resulting electrical signal travels via the cochlear nerve (part of CN VIII) to the auditory cortex.
clinicalNotes: Sensorineural hearing loss is damage to hair cells or the nerve, from noise, ageing (presbycusis), or some drugs (aminoglycosides); hair cells do not regenerate in humans.
A cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells by stimulating the nerve directly with electrodes.
Loud noise exposure over years permanently damages high-frequency hair cells first.

descriptionProfessional: Three fluid-filled loops of the inner ear at right angles to one another. Movement of fluid within them bends hair cells that sense rotation of the head in any plane.
descriptionPatient: Three little looping tubes in your inner ear that sense when your head turns, helping you keep your balance.
apBiologyFacts: Each canal senses rotation in one plane - like the pitch, yaw and roll of an aircraft - by fluid lagging behind the moving head and bending hair cells in the ampulla.
Together with the utricle and saccule (which sense linear acceleration and gravity), they form the vestibular system, which feeds reflexes that keep the eyes steady as the head moves.
Signals travel via the vestibular part of CN VIII to the brainstem and cerebellum.
clinicalNotes: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is brief spinning triggered by head movements, caused by calcium crystals displaced into a canal; the Epley manoeuvre moves them out.
Vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease cause vertigo, nausea and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus).
Spinning then stopping suddenly leaves the fluid still moving, which is why you feel dizzy.

descriptionProfessional: Small bean-shaped filters along lymphatic vessels, in clusters in the neck, armpit, groin and elsewhere. They trap pathogens and cancer cells from lymph and are where lymphocytes meet antigens and mount immune responses.
descriptionPatient: Little bean-sized filters in your neck, armpits and groin that catch germs and help your immune system respond.
apBiologyFacts: Lymph, fluid from tissues, flows through a node's sinuses where macrophages engulf debris and dendritic cells present antigen to B and T lymphocytes, which then multiply (clonal expansion).
Nodes swell during infection because lymphocytes are proliferating inside them.
Lymph flows one way, moved by muscle contraction and valves, and returns to the blood via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct.
clinicalNotes: Tender swollen nodes usually mean a nearby infection; hard, painless, fixed nodes raise concern for cancer.
Cancers spread to lymph nodes first, so removing and examining the nearby (sentinel) node stages breast cancer and melanoma.
Lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes, often presenting as painless enlarged nodes.
